That is so: it is good, I said.

CONCLUSION. By similar reasoning, then, you must grant that one and good are the same. By the same reasoning, she said, you must necessarily grant that one and good are not separate. If you grant two things, you must necessarily grant the third. The syllogism is made like this: what is not good becomes good from the One. So then it has become good from the good! I mean from the One. Therefore one and good are not separate. For things whose effect is not by nature different have the same substance. Things whose action is not separate must have a substance that is not separate. Goodness makes a thing good by its participation in itself, and so does the One. Therefore they have one action. I cannot deny it, I said. I can never deny that, I said.
THAT THE ONE GIVES ALL THINGS THEIR SUBSISTENCE. One? [?] Do you know, then, she said, that everything that exists endures and subsists for as long

as it is [one?] Do you not know, she said, that every one of all things endures and subsists for as long as it is one? But that it perishes and is dissolved as soon as it has ceased to be one? And falls apart and passes away when it is not one? In what way? How, I said, is that so? As, she said, in living creatures: when soul and body come together into one and remain so, that is called a living creature. As you can see, she said, in all living things: when soul and body come together

and live together, that is called a living creature. But when this unity is dissolved by the separation of the two, it is clear that it perishes and is no longer a living creature. When this union comes apart through the separation of the two, the living creature must necessarily perish and no longer exist.
The body itself, too, is seen as a human form as long as it remains in one shape through the joining of its limbs. Even our own body itself

As long as he keeps his form in the joining of his limbs, so long is he like a human being. But if the parts of the body, divided and separated, have pulled its unity apart, it ceases to be what it had been. But if the limbs, separated and taken apart, take away from the body its being one, then what it was perishes. And in this way, to anyone who goes through the other things, it will without doubt be clear that each thing subsists as long as it is one. And look at all other things: then you see each thing endure as long as it is one. But when it ceases to be one, it perishes. And it perishes when it is not one.
"To me, as I consider many things," I said, "nothing else appears." "Wherever I have looked into it," I said, "there I find it so."
QUESTION OF PHILOSOPHY: WHETHER ANYTHING TENDS TOWARD DESTRUCTION. "Is there, then," she said, "anything which, insofar as it acts according to nature, abandons the desire to subsist and
wishes to come to destruction and corruption?" "Is there anything," she said, "that, following nature, willingly gives up being, and wants to perish and decay?"
RESPONSE OF BOETHIUS: THAT ANIMALS DO NOT TEND TOWARD IT; THAT HE IS IN DOUBT ABOUT THE REST. "If I consider animals," I said,

"which have some nature of willing and not willing, I find nothing that, with nothing compelling it from outside, casts off the intention of remaining and hastens of its own accord to destruction." "If I examine living things," I said, "which by nature are able to will and not will, I find none of them that, without outward compulsion, has no desire for being and hastens of its own will to perdition." Outward compulsion is that which some event brings about, such as sicknesses, wounds, persecutions, and calamities. By these a person is often so overcome, often, that life is loathsome to him.
"For every animal labors to protect its well-being,

but avoids death and destruction." "Everything that lives always strives to keep its well-being, and always flees death and destruction." "But what I should grant about plants and trees, and what about wholly inanimate things, I am entirely in doubt." "But what I should say about trees and about plants, which live from sap, and about non-living things, such as stones and metals, about that I am in doubt."

LIKEWISE SHE: THAT NEITHER TREES NOR PLANTS TEND TOWARD IT. "And yet there is no reason for you to be in doubt about this too, when you observe, first, that plants and trees grow in places suited to them, where, as far as their nature allows,
they cannot quickly dry up and perish." "Truly," she said, "you need not doubt even that,

since you see every plant and every tree grow in the place that suits it — I mean where it cannot suddenly wither or perish, as far as nature permits. For some indeed spring up in fields, others on mountains; marshes bear others, others cling to rocks,
and the barren sands are fertile for others.

For each of them grows in its own place: some in the field, some on the mountain, some grow in the fen, some cling to the stones, some stand on sand. If someone tries to move them to other places, they wither. They soon dry up if anyone sets them somewhere else. But nature gives each one what suits it, and works so that they do not perish as long as they can remain. Therefore nature gives each one the place that suits it, and takes care that it always lasts as long as it possibly can.
ON THEIR NOURISHMENT. What of the fact that all of them, as if with their mouths sunk into the earth, draw nourishment through their roots, and through the pith and the bark

spread their strength? What do you say to this? Why do you not see from this how eager they are: as it were, they thrust their beak into the earth and suck the sap with their roots, and from there they distribute it upward as their strength, along the pith and along the bark? What of the fact that whatever is softest, such as the pith, is always hidden in the innermost place, while outside it there is a certain firmness of wood, and the outermost bark is set against the harshness of the sky like a defender who can endure hardship? And what also of this: they hide the softest part, such as the pith, innermost, with the outer firmness of the wood around it, and the bark, like one practiced in hardships, stands outermost as a shield against all weathers?
Now indeed, how great is nature's diligence, that all things, by multiplied seed,

are propagated! For do you not see how attentive nature is to this too, that all growing things are planted far and wide through the abundance of their seed? Who does not know that all these things are like certain machines, made not only to remain for a time but also to remain generation after generation, as if forever? Who does not recognize that all growing things are, as it were, a framework and apparatus, made not only to last for a while but also to endure forever through the succession of generations?

LIKEWISE, THAT INANIMATE THINGS DO NOT TEND TOWARD DESTRUCTION. Do not even the things believed to be inanimate each desire what is their own, for a similar reason? Do not the lifeless things also seek what is their own in the same way?
For why does lightness carry flames upward, while weight presses the earth downward, unless these places and motions suit each of them?

What else does it mean that lightness draws fire upward and heaviness sinks the earth downward, except that the places and the courses suit both of them: downward for the one, upward for the other? Furthermore, whatever is in keeping with each thing preserves that thing. Each of all things always keeps what suits it, just as things that are hostile to it destroy it. So also, on the other hand, it is [?] by those things that are opposed to it. Again, things that are hard, such as stones, cling very tightly to their parts and resist being easily broken apart. Things that are hard, such as stones, hold fast together and do not allow anyone to break them easily. But things that are liquid,
such as air and water, yield easily to whatever divides them, but quickly flow back into the parts from which they were cut off.

But those that are fluid, such as air and water, separate easily and quickly run back together again. But fire flees all cutting. Fire does not separate. That is because it has no density by which it would be a body, nor does it exist through itself, as air and water do, so that it could be divided as they are. In bodies it is just like frost and other accidents: the bodies in which it is are the things that separate. So also is the voice, which comes all together to many ears. It is undivided, though the hearing ears are separate. And it is also corporeal, as Priscian says, because the voice is struck air.

WHAT IS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN NATURAL MOTION AND VOLUNTARY MOTION. Nor are we now dealing with the voluntary motions of the knowing soul, but with natural intention. And understand well that I am not now showing you how gladly each thing exists from the voluntary movements of the rational soul. Rather, I show it to you from natural striving. Nature has its own direction, which no will guides. Just as we digest the food we have taken without thinking, and in sleep we draw breath without knowing it. This shows that we digest our food even though we do not think about it, and that we breathe while sleeping, without knowing it. Therefore nature has its movements without the will.
For not even in animals does the love of remaining come from the wishes of the soul, but from the principles of nature. Not even in living beings...

...is their gladness to exist something they have from the will of the soul. Rather, it took its beginning from nature. For often, when causes compel it, the will embraces death, which nature dreads. This is evident in the fact that a man often wants death for the sake of some need, though nature shuns it. And conversely...
And conversely: the work of begetting, which nature always desires, and by which alone the long duration of mortal things endures, is sometimes restrained by the will.

Sexual union, which nature desires, and from which the long duration of mortal things comes, is often suppressed by the will. Nature fears death, and the will desires it. Nature loves sexual union, and the will refuses it. For this reason she says, "conversely." So far is it from true that this love of self proceeds from animal motion; it proceeds from natural intention. So, certainly, the love of life does not come from the will of the soul, but from the direction of nature. For providence gave to the things it created this as the very greatest cause of remaining: that they naturally desire to remain as long as they can. God's providence gave to its creatures, as the chief cause of their enduring, that they always desire to endure for as long as they can.
Therefore there is nothing you could in any way doubt: all things that exist
naturally desire the constancy of remaining

and avoid destruction. Therefore you need not doubt that all that exists naturally seeks the constancy of enduring and shuns destruction. "I confess," I said, "that I now see without doubt what for a long time seemed uncertain." I confess, said I, that I now recognize with certainty what was uncertain to me before.
"But whatever desires to subsist and remain," she said, "desires to be one."

"And that it wants always to be and to remain," she said, "that desires one being. For if this is taken away, being will not remain for anything. If this is removed, no being is left at all." "That is true," I said. "That is true," I said.
PREMISE. "Therefore," she said, "all things desire one." "Therefore," she said, "they all want one." "I agreed." "I have granted that," I said.
PREMISE. "But we have shown that one is the very same as good." "Now I have also shown you," she said, "that one and good are entirely the same." "So it is." "So you have," I said.
CONCLUSION. "Therefore all things seek the good." "Therefore," she said, "they all seek the good." That syllogism also appears earlier.

DEFINITION OF THE GOOD. "You may indeed describe it like this: the good itself is that which is desired by all." "Now you can give the good," she said, "this definition: That is good which all things desire."

WHAT A DEFINITION IS. Here it should be known that definition is also a proper instrument of the philosophers for disputation, just as argument and syllogism are. It seemed to them that with these three we can be instructed in everything, and that everything else is uncertain unless it is proven to us by arguing, reasoning, and defining. They found sixteen places of arguments and twenty-six modes of reasoning, but for definitions the numbers vary: Cicero teaches us four modes in the Topics, and the rhetorician Victorinus fifteen. Of these fifteen modes, only one is properly called definition.

The others are rather called descriptions. A definition sets out the thing and shows it to us as we see it. A description only indicates it. It is a definition when it shows us the thing substantially, like this: An animal is soul and body. The animal is composed of these two; these two make it. But it is a description when it is only sketched for us what the thing is, like this: An animal is something mobile. Though that is true, it still shows us the animal accidentally, not substantially. Mobility is an accident of the animal. No animal is made out of accidents. Therefore 'descriptio' means painting, marking, and image, as when I scratch the form of an animal on wax with my stylus.

But 'definitio' means marking out boundaries, as when we separate bounds from bounds. It also means 'exact measure', like something measured precisely, so that there is nothing more and nothing less. "Nothing truer can be thought of," I said. "Nothing truer can be devised," I said. "For either all things are referred to nothing and, as if deprived of one head, will drift about without a ruler; or, if there is something
toward which all things hasten, that will be the highest of all goods."

For it must be one of two things: either all things look toward nothing and go astray like headless things, or, if they all hasten toward something, that is necessarily the best of all things. And she said, "I rejoice greatly, O my pupil." And then she said, "Now I am very glad of it, my companion. For you have fixed in your mind the very mark of the central truth. You have made your heart drink in the most central point of the truth."
WHAT THE END OF THINGS IS. "But in this, what you said a little earlier that you did not know has become clear to you."

And from this matter you have learned what you said before you did not know. "What?" I said. "Which is that?" I said. "What the end of all things is," she said. "For that is surely what is desired by all." That is the end that all things strive toward. "Since we have concluded that this is the good for all, we must confess that the end of all things is the good." Since we have proven that the end is good, we must therefore admit that the good is the end of all things.
THAT THE MIND MUST BE QUESTIONED ABOUT ALL TRUTH.
Whoever searches for the truth with a deep mind,
and wishes to be misled by no wrong paths,
let him turn back upon himself, that is, examine, the light of his inner sight. Whoever seeks the true good by thinking deeply,

and does not want to be deceived by false things, let him ask this of his own mind. "And bending his long motions, let him force them into a circle." And bending the long journeys of his mind into the shape of a ring, let him make them go around. That is: let him often turn his mind back to it.
And let him teach his mind
that it possesses, hidden away in its own treasures, whatever it labors at, that is, searches for, outside. And let him teach his mind that it has at home what it seeks elsewhere.
What the dark cloud of error once covered

will shine more clearly than Phoebus himself. If he does that, then what he did not know begins to open up to him, more plainly than the light of the sun. She says this because he should consider for himself how true what she teaches him is. "For the body, bringing in its forgetful mass,"
has not driven all light from the mind.

For the body, which causes forgetfulness, has nevertheless not taken the truth from the mind completely, although it is written: "The body which weighs down the soul oppresses the mind that thinks many things."
Surely the seed of truth clings within,
which is roused when teaching fans it.
Some spark of the truth lies hidden in there, which is brought back to life by teaching blowing upon it. "For why, when asked, do you judge rightly of your own accord, that is, without a teacher,"

"if the tinder did not live, sunk deep in the heart?" Otherwise, why are you so ready to find what is right when someone asks you about it, if the tinder did not lie buried there, deep in the heart? That is an argument from effect. How can there be an effect without the efficient cause?
But if Plato's Muse sounds forth the truth,
then what each person learns, he remembers after having forgotten it.

If Plato's poem speaks truly, everything a person learns after having forgotten it, he is recollecting. Plato and other philosophers believed that the souls of men knew all things before they came into bodies, and that, having become forgetful because of this, they afterward recall them only one at a time. "Then I said: I agree strongly with Plato." I agree very firmly with Plato, I said. "For you are now reminding me of these things for the second time: first because I lost the memory through bodily contagion, that is, mixture, and then when I was weighed down by the mass of grief." For you are now teaching me all this a second time. The first time was because I had fallen into forgetfulness through the pressure of the body, when my master taught it to me in school, and now the second time, because I am burdened by heavy sorrow.
THAT THE WORLD IS GOVERNED BY THE RUDDER OF GOODNESS. Then she said: "If you look back at what was granted earlier, not even that will be far away."

…that you should recall what you confessed a little while ago that you did not know. "If you will think back," she said, "to your earlier admission, then you will quickly manage to remember what you said before that you did not know." "What is that?" said I. "What is that?" said I.
"By what rudders," she said, "the world is governed."

"Which," she said, "is the steering-rudder with which God rules this world." "I remember," said I, "that I confessed my ignorance." "I remember well," said I, "having admitted my ignorance." "But although I already foresee what you are bringing forward, I still want to hear it more plainly from you." "Whatever you mean to say, even though I already know it now, I will still gladly hear it from you."
"A little while ago," she said, "you thought that it was not at all to be doubted that this world is ruled by God." "That God rules this world," she said, "you declared earlier

that you had no doubt." "Nor do I think so now," said I, "nor will I ever think that it is to be doubted." "Nor do I doubt it now," said I, "nor ever." "And by what reasons I arrive at this, I will briefly explain.

And by what reasoning I arrive at it, I will tell you quickly. This world would never have come together into one form out of such diverse and contrary parts, unless there were one who joined such diverse things together. This world would not have united itself into one form out of its parts, so various and so opposed to one another (as water and fire are, and air and earth), if there were not one who fitted such various things together. But the very diversity of natures, once joined, being discordant with itself, would separate and tear apart [the whole],

unless there were one who held together what he had bound. And moreover, once he had fastened them together, the struggling discord of the natures would undo itself and tear itself apart, if there were not one who held together what he had joined. That is a threefold argument: from dissimilars, from things in conflict, from contraries. Dissimilars are body and soul; things in conflict are fire and earth; contraries are fire and water. These would of necessity flee one another if someone did not force them together. Nor indeed would the order of nature proceed so certainly,
nor would [its parts] unfold such well-ordered motions in places, times, effects, intervals, and qualities, unless there were one who, himself remaining unchanged, ordered these varieties of changes.

Nor would the order of nature be so certain, nor would the parts follow such certain courses. Certain in their places: as the moon has, among the planets, the motion nearest the earth, and Saturn the one nearest the heavens. Certain in their times: as the moon's return takes twenty-seven days, and the sun's, on the other hand, three hundred and sixty-five days. Certain in their effects: as the moon, passing in front of the sun, causes an eclipse of the sun, and the sun makes the other planets stationary, or retrograde, or anomalous [?]. Certain in their intervals: as there is always half the sky between the full moon and the sun.

…fixed in their nature, just as the new moon is always horned and the full moon round. None of this would happen at all if there were not one constant being who created these varied changes. That is an argument from effects: the effects teach us about the one who causes them. Whatever this is, by which created things remain and are moved, that is, governed, I call it God, by the name familiar to all. That from which all creatures always exist and by which they are governed, I call God, as is the custom. Then she said: Since you think this way,
I think little effort remains for me before you, possessing happiness, may return safe to your homeland.

Since you know that, she said then, there is hardly anything left for me to do before you return home safe, enjoying happiness. What does she mean by homeland, if not justice and wisdom, for which man was created? Or paradise, from which he was cast out? But let us look at what we have set out. Now let us see what we have agreed on.
PREMISE. Did we not count sufficiency as part of blessedness?
PREMISE. And did we agree that God is blessedness itself? Did I not say earlier that sufficiency is included in blessedness, and that God is that blessedness? Yes, indeed. I did, I said.
CONCLUSION. Then, she said, he will need no outside aids to rule the world.

Since that is so, she said, he has no need of outside help to rule the world, because he has it in himself. The syllogism runs like this: Sufficiency is in blessedness. God is blessedness. Therefore God is sufficient to rule the world. Otherwise, if he needed anything, he would not have full sufficiency. Put another way: if he lacks anything, he is not sufficient. This is an argument from the part, because whoever lacks something does not have the whole.

That, I said, must necessarily be so. It must be so, I said. Then he arranges all things by himself alone. By himself, directly, he orders things. That cannot be denied, I said. There can be no denying it, I said.
LIKEWISE. But God has been shown to be the good itself. Now God has also been said to be good, she said.
I remember, I said. I remember it well, I said. Then he arranges all things through the good itself, since he rules all things through himself,

and we agreed that he is good. If he who is himself good governs by himself, then he governs by the good. That is an argument from the name, that is, from interpretation. Because "God" and "good" are pluriuoca [?], whatever is done by God is done by the good. And this is, as it were, a kind of tiller and rudder by which the machinery of the world is kept stable and unspoiled. And this is the peg and the helm by which the structure of the world is kept steady and unharmed. Whoever steers seagoing ships does not put his hand on the steering oar itself, but only on the peg that is on the oar. He turns that, as we also see
on some lakes. I agree completely, I said, and I saw a little while ago that you would say this, though I only faintly suspected it.

"I agree with you on that in earnest," I said, "and I knew beforehand, from the way things were going, that you would say so. I perceived it, though I barely perceived it." "I believe it," she said, "for now, I think, you are turning your eyes more watchfully to discern the truth." "I believe," she said, "that you perceived it beforehand, because now, I think, you have more wakeful eyes for discerning the truth."

ALL THINGS IN ACCORD WITH NATURE ARE GOVERNED WILLINGLY. "But what I shall say next is no less open to view. What I still want to say, you can see just as plainly." "What?" I said. "What is that?" I said.

"Since God," she said, "is rightly believed to govern all things with the rudder of goodness, and all these same things, as I have taught, hasten toward the good by a natural striving, can there be any doubt

that they are ruled willingly? When God rules things," she said, "with the rudder of goodness, and they all strive toward goodness, can there then be any doubt that they are willing to be ruled? And that they turn of their own accord at the nod of the one who orders them, as being in harmony with their ruler and attuned to him? And do they not turn gladly according to the master's will, as if they were in agreement with their ruler and set in order toward him?"

"It must be so," I said. "It is necessarily so," I said. "Nor would it seem a blessed rule if it were a yoke on the resisting rather than the salvation of the obedient. Nor would that ruling be blessed

if it were the coercion of the resisting rather than the salvation of the obedient. Because resistance would be against nature, it would therefore not have a blessed end. This is an argument from cause: things that keep to their nature have a good end. That is why Paul said: 'You have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life.' Sanctification is in accord with nature; therefore it is the cause of eternal life. Eternal life is its end. There is therefore nothing that, while keeping its nature, tries to go against God. Therefore nothing that keeps its nature is opposed to God." "Nothing," I said. "Nothing," I said.
RESISTANCE ACHIEVES NOTHING. "What if something should try?" she said. "What," she said, "if some creature attempts it, as the giants did and as all the wicked do?
Could it in the end achieve anything against him whom we have agreed is most powerful by right of blessedness?

Can it then do anything against the most powerful one, whom I acknowledged to be most powerful through blessedness?" "It would achieve absolutely nothing," I said. "Nothing at all," I said. "There is therefore nothing that would either want or be able to resist this highest good!" (that is, because the wicked are nothing). "Therefore there is nothing," she said, "that can or will stand against the highest good." "I think not," I said.
"I do not believe so," I said. "It is therefore the highest good that rules all things mightily and orders them sweetly."

"Therefore," she said, "the good is the highest, which creates all things gently and mightily." Then I said: "How greatly they delight me, not only the conclusion your arguments have reached, but much more these very words that you use." Then I said: "How delightful to me is not only the substance of the argument that you have concluded for me, but even more the words that you speak." She speaks beautifully here, and also where she speaks of herself: "Wisdom reaches from end to end mightily, and orders all things sweetly." "You have heard in the fables," she said, "of the giants assailing heaven. But them too, as was fitting, a kindly strength put in order.
so that at last folly, tearing at great things, that is, provoking God,

may be ashamed of itself." "You have read in the fable," she said, "that the giants fought against heaven: Otus and Ephialtes, the sons of Neptune, who grew nine fingers every month. But God's power repaid them, as was just, for they were all struck down with thunderbolts." That warns the arrogant scoffers [?] who provoke God that they should at some point refrain from it. Phlegra is the name of the giants' city in Thessaly, where the mighty stones still lie, many of them scattered across the field; the fables say the giants fought against heaven with them. But the ones who truly did this were those who after the Flood built a tower against God, and they were divided by languages.
THAT EVIL IS NOTHING. "But would you have us strike the arguments themselves against one another?
Perhaps from a clash of this kind some beautiful spark of truth may leap out."

"Would you like me now," she said, "to strike together the very arguments I have shown before, so that some beautiful spark springs out of them?" "As you judge best," I said. "As you wish," I said. "No one would doubt," she said, "that God is all-powerful." "No one doubts," she said, "that God is almighty."
"No one at all who is of sound mind," I said, "would doubt it." "Whoever is sensible," I said, "does not doubt it." "But he who is all-powerful," she said,
"is there anything he cannot do?" "He who can do everything," she said, "can there be anything he cannot do?" "Nothing," I said. "Nothing," I said. An argument from the whole to the part.
"Can God, then, do evil?" "Can God do evil?" she said.

"By no means," I said. "No," I said. "Then evil is nothing," she said, "since he who can do everything cannot do it." "Therefore," she said, "evil is nothing, since he who can do everything cannot do it." An argument from the efficient cause. Where is the effect if the one who brings it about does not exist? That is the spark: that evil is nothing. For this reason Augustine says that evil is not a creature, nor a work of God, but a falling away from God. For angel and man to fall away from God and not to cling to him is evil.
ON THE LIKENESS OF THESE ARGUMENTS. "Are you playing with me," I said, "weaving out of arguments a labyrinth that cannot be escaped?

"Are you playing with me," I said, "with your words, building such an intricate labyrinth? Now you go in where you came out, and now you come out where you went in?" That is, now you go in where you went out, and again you go out where you went in. That is how it goes in a labyrinth, and as you can see here. "Or are you folding together some wonderful circle of divine simplicity?" Or are you winding the wonderful ball of thread of God's simplicity?
"For a little earlier, beginning from beatitude, you said that it was the highest good, which you said was situated in the highest God.

This is how you have spoken with me: you began with beatitude, said that it was the highest good, and said that it was in God. "You also argued that God himself is the highest good and full beatitude." And you said that God himself is the highest good and also beatitude. "From this you gave me, as a little gift, that no one would be blessed unless he were likewise God." And from that you told me, as a gift, that no one is blessed unless he is God together with him. At that point you came out at beatitude, where you had also begun. "Again you said that the very form of the good is the substance of God and of beatitude."

And again, beginning at beatitude where you had left off, you said that the image of the highest good is the substance of God and of beatitude. "And you taught that the one itself is that very good which is sought by the whole nature of things." And you said that the one good is what all things seek. "You also argued that God rules the universe with the helm of goodness." And you said that God steers the whole world with the rudder of goodness. "That all things willingly obey." And that all things willingly yield to him. "And that there is no nature of evil." And that there is no nature of evil. These are the things that you said and that you have woven into one another. "And you set these out with no proofs taken from outside, but with inherent and domestic ones, each drawing its credibility from another." And you have set them all out with proper and inherent arguments, not with foreign ones, and in such a way that each of them receives credibility from another. God and good, blessedness and one: there are four of these, and each of them strengthened the other.

ON ARGUMENTS. Here it must be understood very carefully which arguments are taken from within (intrinsecus) and which from outside (extrinsecus). Those that are taken from the affecta, that is, from attached things, are the ones taken from within. Aristotle counts sixteen of these affecta: whole, parts, notation, conjugates, genus, species, similar, dissimilar, adjuncts, contrary, antecedent, consequent, contradictory, cause, effect, and comparable. These are attached and inherent to the things about which one disputes or has doubts. Where else can a question be worked out, if it is worked out by art, except from one of these? The whole is argued from the part, and the part from the whole.

…or from nota (the sign or name), if it has a nota. Which things have a nota without pluriuoca (several words for one thing)? Therefore whatever one ascribes to ensis (sword), one ascribes to gladius (sword). If an ensis strikes him, then a gladius strikes him. If locuples (a wealthy man) strikes him, then dives (a rich man) strikes him. If Scipio does it, then Africanus does it. It goes the same way with the divine names. Deus (God), bonum (the good), unum (the one), beatum (the blessed) work together. Whatever is predicated of one of them is predicated of all of them, because none of them has anything more intrinsic [?] than that it is always the very same. In the same way a coniugatum (a word of the same root) is inferred from another word of its own family. Genus from species, species from genus.

Like from like, unlike from unlike, adjunct from adjunct, contrary from contrary, antecedent from consequent, consequent from antecedent, incompatible from incompatible, cause from effect, effect from cause, comparable from comparable. But those arguments that are not taken from things attached to the matter, but from testimonies, rumours, quaestiones, that is, extortions (torture), meaning from confessions, from lots, from dreams, and from other things like these, are called extrinsecus sumpta (taken from outside). They are also called artis expertia (lying outside the art), because they are not worked out by reasoning,

but learned by asking. When the question is, "Will the dead rise again?", I do not look to any of the sixteen topics listed, because this cannot be known by the art. It is known by the testimony of Christ, who promised this: "Amen, I say to you, the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and will come forth." It goes the same way with the other external topics. An argumentum is a proof, as when we say, "If this is, then that is." But if we say, "If these two are, then that third will be," that is called ratiocinatio in Latin and syllogismus in Greek.

AGAIN, ON THE SINGLE FORM OF THE GODHEAD. Then she said: "We are not playing at all, and by the gift of God, to whom we prayed a little while ago, we have worked out the greatest matter of all." Then she said: "No, I am not playing with you, as you claim. By God's leave I have explained to you the greatest of all things. We entreated him before, namely with the verses 'O qui perpetua mundum ratione gubernas' ('O you who govern the world by everlasting reason'). The greatest of all things is this: what the highest good is, and what makes a person blessed. Socrates could not find it, nor could all the philosophers after him, even when they searched for it diligently, as Augustine says in the eighth book of The City of God. And with this we have also come to recognize the simplicity of God, who holds goodness and blessedness in himself in such a way

that they are one with him. So when he is described by them, or they by him, this description is not extrinsecus sumpta (taken from outside), because they are not in him accidentally but substantially. For such is the form, that is, the nature, of the divine substance, that it neither slips away into external things nor takes anything external into itself. The nature of God's substance is such that it does not change into something else, as Lot's wife was changed into a pillar of salt! Nor does it let anything else into itself, as a person takes on anger and joy, frost and [?] heat. But as Parmenides says of it: "on every side like the mass [?] of a well-rounded sphere."

...turns the moving sphere of things while it keeps itself unmoving. Rather, as the philosopher Parmenides said of it in Greek: it turns all that exists, but it does not move itself. But if we have also put forward arguments that were not sought from outside, but placed within the compass of the matter we were treating, there is no reason for you to wonder, since you have learned, as Plato decreed,

that words must be akin to the things of which they speak. "I also carried on the argument," she said, "not with reasons I took from elsewhere, but with those I found in the very thing I was speaking about. Do not wonder at this, for it is fitting, as Plato taught you, that words be bound to the things of which they are spoken." She says this because, since she spoke of God, she took her arguments from the good, from the one, and from blessedness, which are the same thing. What words cling so closely to God as those spoken of the highest good, of blessedness and of unity, which are his marks (notae)? Since arguments and syllogisms are taken from a mark (nota), the marks are always words akin to the things, because they are taken from within, as was said before.
HAVING FOUND THE LIGHT, ONE MUST NOT RETURN TO THE DARKNESS. Happy is he who has been able to behold the shining fountain of the good,
that is, to see the highest good.

happy is he who has been able to loose the chains of heavy earth, that is, to overcome the burden of the flesh. Blessed is he who has beheld the pure source of all good and has overcome the earthly burden.
After the Thracian bard, once lamenting the death of his wife,
had compelled with mournful measures
the moving woods to run
and the rivers to stand still. When long ago Orpheus, the musician from Thrace, lamenting his wife's death with songs of mourning, made the forest walk and the rivers stand still,
and the hind laid her fearless flank beside the lions,
nor did the hare fear the dog it saw,
now made calm by the song. And the hind went boldly with the lions, nor did the hare fear the hound, both made quiet by the song.
When a more burning passion burned the inmost depths of his breast,
and the measures that had subdued all things did not
soothe their master, that is, Orpheus himself,
complaining of the merciless gods above,

he went to the dwellings of the underworld. When afterwards he suffered still more bitterly for his wife, and his songs, which had made all things tame, did not comfort him, he called the gods of heaven merciless and went to the gods of hell.
There, tempering coaxing songs
on sounding strings,
whatever he had drawn from the foremost springs, that is, from the teachings of his mother the goddess,
what powerless grief gave,
[supply:] powerless to obtain what it wished; what love gave, that is, dictated, redoubling the grief,
he weeps, moving Taenarus. And there, plucking sweetly sounding string-music, the finest he had learned from his mother Calliope,
the Muse, and what his grief, which could achieve little, urged him to, and what his love for his wife taught him, which prompted his weeping: this he sang and wept, until hell grew weary of it.
And with sweet prayer he asks pardon of the lords of the shades. And so sweetly he begged mercy of the lords of the souls.
The three-headed doorkeeper is stunned,
that is, Cerberus, the hellish dog, captured, that is, enticed, by the new song. The three-headed doorkeeper was astonished at such unaccustomed song.
The avenging goddesses of crimes, that is, the three Furies, Allecto, Megaera, Tisiphone, who drive the guilty with fear,

now, sorrowful, are wet with tears. And the three vengeance-eager sisters, who make the damned people fearful, wept for sorrow. What are the Furies but the conscience of the wicked? That is what hunts them.

The swift wheel does not hurl Ixion's head down. Nor did the wheel drive Ixion downward in the meantime. Ixion was king of the Lapiths. He swore [?] in hell that he wanted to sleep with Juno. Therefore he had to push a wheel up a mountain, and he struggled with it, but he never succeeded. That is an example of those who struggle with the world, which always goes downward and carries its followers along with it.
And Tantalus, ruined by long thirst,

scorns the rivers. And Tantalus, who was parched with thirst, then paid no heed to the water. He gave his son Pelops as a young sacrificial animal for the gods and goddesses to eat, to test their divinity. Therefore he stood thirsty in the water and yet could never drink of it. Whoever tests God should fare no better.
While the vulture, sated with the measures [of song],
did not tear at the liver of Tityus.

And, sated with song, the vulture meanwhile did not eat Tityus's liver. He wanted to sleep with Latona, Jupiter's wife. Apollo avenged that, together with Diana, Latona's daughter, by having the vulture eat his liver; and as much as it ate, so much grew back again. The fable warns us of this: that lust, whose seat is in the liver, is not extinguished once it is satisfied, but breaks out afresh again.
The judge of the shades, that is, Vulcan, who is also Ops and Pluto, at last taking pity, says: "We are overcome."
"We grant the man his wife as his companion,
bought by song." At last, said the god of hell, because he too was moved to pity by it: "What more can we do? Let us give the man his wife as a reward for his song."
"But let a law restrain the gift." But on these terms, with this condition, and with this stipulation:
"That until he has left Tartarus
it shall not be permitted to turn his eyes back." That as he goes away from here he must not look behind him.
Who would give a law to lovers?

Love is a greater law unto itself. Who can make rules for love? Love itself makes its own rule. As Virgil said: "For what limit can there be to love?" And again he said: "Love conquers all." For there is also a proverb: where love is, there is the eye. So listen to how it turned out.
Alas, near the borders of night
Orpheus looked at his Eurydice,
lost her, and perished. Ah, too grievously! When he had brought her near the light, there he looked at her, there he lost her, there he himself fell.
This fable concerns you,
all of you who seek to lead the mind into the upper day, that is, to God. This tale looks to you, who undertake to turn the mind
toward the day above. For whoever, overcome (that is, by the desires of the flesh), turns his eyes to the cave of Tartarus, while he looks upon the underworld,

…loses whatever excellent thing he draws with him. For whoever has devoted himself to striving toward that [higher light], and then looks back again toward hell, following his desires, loses by looking there the precious thing he had won, that is, spiritual goods. As it says in the Gospel: "No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God."
ON THE VARIETY OF THE DISPUTATION CARRIED OUT. Just as we should take note of how Boethius in the first book was accusing Fortune,

and how Philosophy defended Fortune against this in the second book with a rhetorical defence, so here in the third book we should note that, because Philosophy speaks by way of disputation, the disputation is threefold. In the second book she began to dispute against riches, honour, power, glory and pleasure. She completed that disputation here in the third book, where she has said that happiness is not found in these things when they are separated from one another. Because she did this by reproving people's morals, the disputation is called moral, in Greek "ethics". After that she shows that happiness is in God, and how the five goods, which human error tries to separate, are found together in him. With that she has answered the chief question of ethics.

For Socrates, with whom that part of philosophy began, and all his followers, who saw people striving for happiness, could not work out where happiness had its place. And although they said, "Happiness consists in attaining the highest good," they were not granted to know what that highest good itself was. From that question she comes to the physical, that is natural, disputation, on the question of whether anything tends toward its own destruction. From there, at the end of the book, she turns again to the theological disputation, where she shows the simplicity of God. HERE ENDS THE THIRD BOOK OF BOETHIUS.
HERE BEGINS THE FOURTH BOOK. QUESTION: WHY THE WICKED REIGN UNDER GOD, WHO IS A GOOD RULER. When Philosophy had sung these things gently and sweetly, keeping the dignity of her face
and the gravity of her mouth, that is, according to the rules of rhetoric, I broke in on her as she was preparing to say something more, for I had not yet entirely forgotten my deep-rooted grief.

When Philosophy sang like this, gently and kindly, with a seemly face and a modest mouth, I interrupted what she still wanted to say, since I was still unconsoled in my sorrow. "O forerunner of the true light," I said, "the things your speech has poured out up to now have shown themselves invincible, both by their own divine contemplation and by your arguments." "Herald of the true light," I said, "whatever you have said up to now is divine in itself, that is, because it leads to God, and is beyond doubt because of your words, since you strengthened it with proofs."
"And you have told me things which I had recently forgotten because of the grief of the wrong done to me, but which were not entirely unknown to me before."

"And you have told me what was not wholly unknown to me before, though I had forgotten it now because of my sorrow. But the greatest cause of our sorrow is this very thing: that evil can exist at all, or go unpunished, while there is a good ruler of the world." "But this same thing makes me saddest: that evil can exist, or go unpunished, since the ruler is good."
You surely see how much wonder this alone deserves. You know well how great a wonder this may rightly be to me. But to this another, greater thing is added. So there is another, even greater wonder.
For while wickedness rules and flourishes, virtue not only goes without rewards but is even trampled under the feet of the wicked,

and pays the penalties in place of crimes. I mean that while vices rule and prosper, virtue not only goes without thanks but is even trodden under the feet of the wicked, and suffers torments in place of the evil. No one can wonder at or lament enough that these things should happen in the kingdom of God, who knows all things and can do all things, but wills only the good. That things should go this way in the kingdom of God, who knows all, is able to do all, and wills only good: no one can fully wonder at this or lament it.
RESPONSE: THAT IT DOES NOT HAPPEN SO, BUT THAT THE MATTER IS TURNED TO THE CONTRARY. Then she said: "And it would be a cause of endless astonishment,

and more horrible than any monster, if in the well-ordered house of so great a householder the base vessels were cared for, as you suppose, while the precious ones were left to grow filthy." "It would also be very astonishing," she said, "and worse than all terrors, if in the house of so mighty a lord, which is ordered in all things, worthless vessels were valued and precious vessels were held worthless.
But it is not so. For if the things we concluded a little while ago are kept unshaken, then with the help of the very author whose kingdom we are now speaking of,
you will come to know that the good are always powerful, while the wicked are always cast down and weak.

If you remember well what I established for you before, you will learn, with the help of God, whose kingdom we are speaking of, that the good are always mighty and the wicked always cast off and powerless. You will learn that vices are never without punishment, nor virtues without reward, and that happy things always befall the good and unhappy things the wicked. Nor are the vicious without torment, nor the virtuous without their reward, and blessings always follow the good, misfortunes the wicked. And you will learn many things of this kind, which will put your complaints to rest and strengthen you with firm solidity. And I will give you many examples of this, which will silence your complaint and give you great confidence. And since a while ago you saw the form of happiness as I showed it to you, you have also learned where it is located.

When I have gone through everything I think it necessary to set out first, I will show you the way that may carry you back home. And since you know from my showing what happiness is like and where it is, after that, once I have first said all that seems good to me, I will also show you the way that brings you home. Where was the form of happiness shown? It is in the definition that he found and that she praised him for, when he said: "Unless I am mistaken, that is true and perfect happiness which makes a person self-sufficient, powerful, worthy of reverence, renowned, and joyful." She showed him that same happiness in God. That is its dwelling place.
I will also fasten wings to your mind.

…by which it can raise itself on high. I will also fasten onto your mind the wings with which it can fly up. So that, once your distress is driven away, you may return safe to your homeland, under my guidance, by my path, and in my vehicles too. So that you may come home safe and free of all cares, as I guide you, along my way, in my chariot.
WHERE THE HOMELAND IS, TO WHICH HE IS TO BE LED, IS SHOWN.
For I have swift wings
that climb to the heights of the sky. "I have," she said, "the wings," that is, the merits of the virtues, which climb swiftly to heaven.
When the swift mind puts them on,
it looks down on the earth with loathing. And as soon as the swift mind puts them on, earthly things at once become hateful to it. She may well say this, for nothing is as swift as the mind.
It rises above the sphere of the boundless air
and sees the clouds behind its back. And it passes over the whole expanse of the wide air and sees the clouds beneath it. And it rises above the summit of the fire
that glows from the swift motion of the ether.

And it climbs above the hot fire of the upper air, which burns from the speed of its motion. In that fire we see at night the shooting fires, which deceive people's eyes so much that they think stars are falling from heaven.
Until it rises into the star-bearing houses
and joins its paths to Phoebus. Until it comes to the place where the planets travel, and rises level with the sun, which is in the middle of the planets.
Or it goes along the path of the cold old man

as a soldier of the gleaming star. Or it makes itself equal to the star of Saturn, which is the highest of the planets. Saturn is named after the old and cold Saturn, either because of the slowness of the thirty years in which it goes around the sky, or because it has a pale colour. The mind has then become a retainer of the true sun, that is, Christ, just as the planets are the retainers of the visible sun. They are its soldiers because it sets their courses for them and makes them stationary, retrograde, or anomalous, and makes them linger a long time near its turnings [?] before they come into sight again. Or it runs back along the circle of the stars
wherever the gleaming night is painted.
Or else, having climbed higher, it reaches the sky itself. I mean the firmament, which is the common ring of all the other stars that shine on a clear night.
And when it has gone far enough,
let it leave the outermost pole behind
and tread on the back of the swift ether, that is, the firmament,
sharing in the awesome light.

And when it has climbed high enough, let it leave the outermost heaven beneath it and tread on the top of the circling firmament, and there enjoy the most glorious light, which it sees in God himself. Here the Lord of kings holds the sceptre
and controls the reins of the world. There the Lord of all kings sits with his sceptre.
And he pulls in the bridle of the world's structure and lets it go slack. And, himself unmoving, he steers the swift chariot,
the shining judge of all things. And, himself at rest, he steers the swift chariot, the beautiful judge of all things.
If the way brings you back here, that is, to this homeland,
which you now seek, having forgotten it, you will say:
"I remember; this is my homeland."

The road leads you there, to that same place which you now long for. There you will say: "Here I recognize myself; here I am at home." "From here I sprang; here I will stand fast." From here I come; here I shall remain.
But if it should please you to look back on the night of earth that you left behind, you will see the grim tyrants as exiles,
those whom the wretched peoples fear.
If you then want to look back here, at the darkness of the world that you left, you will see in exile the terrible rulers whom many wretched people now fear.
THAT THOSE WHO CANNOT OBTAIN WHAT THEY DESIRE ARE NOT POWERFUL. Then I said. Then I answered her.
"Oh," I said, "what great things you promise!" "Oh," I said, "how far your promises reach!"

"And I do not doubt that you can carry it out. Only do not keep waiting the man you have roused." I do not doubt either that you can achieve it. Only do not make me wait now for what you have led me to hope for.
"First, then," she said, "you will be able to see that power is always present to the good, and that the wicked are abandoned by all strength."

"Now," she said, "you must know this first of all: powers are always granted to the good, and the wicked have no strength to act. Each of these is proved from the other." Each of these two statements is strengthened by the other. "For since good and evil are contraries, if it is established that the good is powerful, the weakness of evil is clear." Because good and evil are opposed to each other, if the good man is certainly powerful, then the powerlessness of the wicked is plain. "And if the frailty of evil becomes clear, the firmness of the good is known." Likewise, if the frailty of the wicked is plain to see, then the firmness of the good is evident from it. Whatever is affirmed of the one must be denied of the other. This is because, as she herself says, good and evil are contraries of each other. Therefore this argument is also called

one that she makes "from contraries" (a contrariis). "But to make our position more fully convincing, I will go by both paths, confirming my propositions now from this side and now from that." And so that my argument may be all the more believable to you, let me support what I have put forward by turns: sometimes from the one side, that is, the good, and sometimes from the other, that is, the wicked.
THAT NOTHING IS ACCOMPLISHED WITHOUT ABILITY AND WILL. "There are two things on which every result of human actions depends: will and power." There are two things

by which all works are accomplished: will and power. "If either of them is missing, nothing can be carried out." If either of them is lacking, none of these things can be brought about. "For when the will is missing, no one even undertakes what he does not want." If the will is not there, a man does not even begin what he does not want to do. "But if the power is absent, the will is in vain." If the power is not there, the will achieves nothing. This is an argument from the cause (a causa). How can an effect come about without a cause?
"So it follows that if you see someone wanting to obtain something that he does not obtain at all, you cannot doubt that he lacked the strength to obtain what he wanted." Therefore you can be certain

...that when a man does not obtain what he wanted to obtain, he was not able to obtain it. "It is clear," I said. "That is plain," said I. "Nor can it be denied in any way." "There can be no denying it." "But the one whom you see to have accomplished
what he wished, will you doubt that he was also able to?

"And the one who succeeds in what he desires," said she, "should you doubt his power?" "Not at all." "No," said I. "But what each person can do, in that he is to be judged strong; and what he cannot do, in that he is to be judged weak." "Therefore," said she, "a man is to be considered powerful in what he can do, and powerless in what he cannot do." "I admit it," I said. "I grant you that," said I.

THE GOOD ARE POWERFUL, BUT THE WICKED ARE WEAK. "Do you remember, then," she said, "that it was concluded by the earlier arguments that every intention of the human will, which is driven by different pursuits, hastens toward happiness?" "Now do you remember," said she, "that it was established above by syllogism that the will of all men, which strives after various things, aims at happiness?" "I remember," I said, "that this too was demonstrated."

"I know that this too was said before," said I. "Do you recall that happiness is the good itself, and that in this way, when happiness is sought, the good is desired by all?" "Do you not remember," said she, "that happiness is the good, and that in this way all who desire happiness desire the good?"
"I do not [merely] recall it," I said,

"since I keep it fixed in memory." "No," said I, "I do not [need to] recall it, because I hold it in mind." "Therefore all men, good and bad alike, strive with an undistinguished intention to reach the good." "Therefore," said she, "all men hasten, aiming alike toward the good, whether they are good or bad." "So it follows," I said. "That follows necessarily from it," said I. "But it is certain that people become good by obtaining the good." "Now it is also certain," said she, "that people become good by obtaining good." "Certain." "Certain," said I. "Do the good, then, obtain what they seek?" "Do the good, then," said she, "obtain what they long for?" "So it seems." "So it seems to me," said I. "But if the wicked obtained the good they seek, could they still be wicked?"

"If the wicked too obtained the good that they desire," said she, "would they not then cease to be wicked?" "That is so." "That is so," said I. "Since, then, both seek the good, but the one group obtains it and the other does not, is there any doubt that the good are powerful and those who are wicked are weak?" "Since they are both seekers of the good," said she, "and the one group obtains it while the other does not obtain it, are not the good, who obtain it, powerful, and the wicked powerless?" This is an argument from the end (argumentum a fine). From the end, that is, from obtaining or not obtaining, efficacy or inefficacy becomes apparent, that is to say, power or weakness. "Whoever doubts this," I said,

"can consider neither the nature of things nor the logical consequence of arguments." "Whoever doubts that," said I, "does not understand the nature of things, nor which statement follows necessarily from another."

WHAT THE NATURE OF THINGS IS, AND THE CONSEQUENCE OF REASONINGS. The nature of things is what she herself teaches soon after, in the next chapter: that happiness is won through virtue, which is good. Happiness is good, and none of it is achieved through the vices, which are not good. Nature is found in good things, such as virtue. No nature is found in vices, only the corruption of nature. Therefore virtue is powerful;

vices are powerless. By looking at nature, one learns the consequence of reasonings. As Aristotle teaches in the Peri Hermeneias, where does the consequence of reasonings come from, if not from the consequence of things? What is true of things is also true of reasonings. Power goes together with virtue, and the effect of the will goes together with power. That is where this consequence of reasonings comes from, so that one can say: Where there is virtue, there is also power; and where there is power, there is the effect of the will. Sixteen places of arguments show us the consequence of reasonings. As Cicero says in the Topics, the consequence stays unchanged in only three places; in the others it varies. The ones that do not vary always carry the necessity of truth. The ones that vary show sometimes the necessity of truth,

and sometimes only the likelihood of truth. Which ones do not vary? They are the arguments from antecedents, from consequents, and from contraries. From antecedents: 'If she has lain with a man, she is not a virgin.' Lying with a man always comes before not being a virgin. From consequents: 'If she has given birth, she has lain with a man.' Giving birth comes after lying with a man. From contraries: 'She has not both lain with a man and remained a virgin.' Lying with a man and virginity cannot exist together. These are true arguments, and all arguments drawn from these places are true in the same way. But those that come from other places

are sometimes necessary and sometimes only probable. This can be seen in these two arguments from cause: 'If there is fire, it is hot.' 'If she is a mother, she loves her son.' The first is always true. The second is believable, because it is usually so. Because the first is true at all times, it is true to say at all times. But because the second is only sometimes true, it is only sometimes true to say. In this way the consequence of reasonings always follows the consequence of things, and what is found in things is true to say. Therefore the nature of things always gives reasonings their truth.
WHAT HOLDS THE WICKED BACK, SO THAT THEY DO NOT REACH THE APPOINTED END AS THE GOOD DO. Again, she said. Again, she said: If there are two people
who have the same purpose according to nature, and one of them does and accomplishes that very thing by its natural function, while the other is entirely unable to perform

that natural function, and in a way that does not suit nature does not actually fulfil his purpose but only imitates the one who fulfils it, which of these do you judge to be stronger? If there are two people who are both willing to do one thing naturally, and one of them does it naturally, and the other cannot do it that way and strives at it in another way, by which he still does not do it but only imitates the one who does it, which of them do you think is more capable?
"Even so," I said, "I can guess what you mean.

but I want to hear it more plainly." "Though I may well guess what you mean," I said, "I would still gladly understand it more openly." "The motion of walking," she said, "is natural to human beings. Will you deny it?" "That people are able to walk," she said, "do you deny that this is natural?" "Not at all," I said. "No," said I. "And that the function of this belongs naturally to the feet, do you doubt it?" "Do you doubt, then, that this is the natural office of the feet?" "Not this either," I said.
"Not that either," said I. "If, then, someone who is able to go on his feet walks, and another, who lacks this natural function of the feet,
tries to walk by leaning on his hands, which of these can rightly be thought the stronger?" Whoever walks with the use of his feet,

and another, who does not have the use of them, strives to walk by leaning on his hands: which of them seems to you the mightier? "Go on with the rest," I said. "Just tell me more," said I. "For no one doubts that a person who is capable of a natural function is stronger than one who cannot perform it." For no one doubts that the one who has control of a natural office is the mightier
than the one who does not. "But the highest good is set before the wicked and the good alike. The good seek it through the natural function of the virtues,
while the wicked try to obtain that very same thing through various desires, which is not the natural way of obtaining the good." Now the good, she said, seek the highest good,

which is offered equally to both the good and the wicked, by means of the office of the virtues. But the wicked strive to win it with various worldly cravings, which are no natural office for winning the good. "Or do you think otherwise?" Does it seem otherwise to you? "Not at all," I said. "No," said I. "For what follows from this is also clear. From the things I have granted," That too is clear, said I, namely what follows from this.
it necessarily follows that the good are powerful and the wicked weak.

For according to these words of yours, which I have assented to, the good are necessarily mighty and the wicked powerless. "You are rightly running ahead of me," she said, "and that is a sign, as physicians usually hope, of a nature that is now restored and resisting," that is, recovering from sickness. You are rightly anticipating me, she said, and that is a token of your recovery, as physicians believe. When a physician tells a sick man how he will recover, and the sick man understands it and even speaks ahead of him, that is a sign that his health is coming back.

HOW VERY GREAT A THING IT IS IN WHICH THE WICKED FAIL. "But since I see that you are most ready to understand, I will pile up argument after argument." Because I see that you are so quick to understand, I will give you reasons enough.

"For see how plainly the weakness of vicious men shows itself. They cannot even reach the thing that natural inclination leads them toward and almost compels them to reach." See how great the powerlessness of the wicked is: they cannot even come to the place that natural striving leads them to, and even almost drags them to.

"And what if they were left without this great and almost invincible help of nature going before them?" What would become of them if they lacked such great and almost unfailing help from nature, which guides them?
"But consider how great a powerlessness holds wicked men in its grip.

Now consider carefully what weaknesses the wicked have. For the rewards they seek, and cannot reach or obtain, are not light or trivial. For these are not light or laughable things that they cannot win and cannot reach. Rather, they fail in the very sum and summit of things. Rather, they fall short in the highest thing of all, where the head of all things is. Nor do these wretches achieve the one thing they work at day and night. And the one thing they toil for, by day and by night, they do not succeed in.
HOW FAR THE GOOD EXCEL IN THIS: THAT THE WICKED CANNOT RESIST VICES.
In this matter the strength of the good stands out. At this point the powers of the good come to the fore. For just as you would judge that man the most powerful at walking
who, going on foot, could reach the place beyond which there was no further way to go,
so you must judge that man the most powerful who grasps the end of all things to be desired,

beyond which there is nothing. Just as you would say that a walker has full command of his walking if he went so far that there was no more road beyond, so you rightly call that man mighty who stretches himself until he reaches the very end of all that is to be desired. He is blessed for this reason: there is nothing further left for him to desire. From this follows the opposite: that the wicked also appear to be stripped of all strength. From this follows what is unlike it, I mean that the wicked are without any powers.
Why else would they abandon virtue and pursue vices?

Why, then, do they love vices more than virtues? Is it from ignorance of what is good? Is it that they do not know what is good? But what is more feeble than the blindness of ignorance? Then what can be more cowardly than ignorance? Or do they know what they ought to follow, but desire throws them headlong off course? Or do they know the better course, and their desires drive them off course, as a wind blowing crosswise drives a ship out of control? In that case too they are made frail by lack of self-control, since they cannot struggle against vice. In that case too they are worthless, since they cannot master themselves or defend themselves against vices.
THAT THE WICKED, BY WILLINGLY DESERTING THE GOOD, ARE REDUCED TO NOTHING.
Or do they desert the good knowingly and willingly, and turn aside to vices?

Shall we say that they leave the good knowingly and willingly, and attach themselves to evil? But in this way they cease not only to be powerful but to exist at all. If that is so, then they lose not only their power but even their very being. For those who abandon the common end of all things that exist also cease to exist. Those who forsake what is the common end of all that exists have given up being. If they do not hold to what is the end, where else can they go?

It may perhaps seem strange to someone that I say the wicked, who make up the greater part of humankind, do not exist. It may perhaps seem a wonder to some that I say those people do not exist who are the most numerous of all. But that is how the matter stands. But it is so nonetheless. For those who are wicked,
I do not deny that they are wicked.

But that they simply and without qualification are, I deny. That they are evil, I do not deny. That they exist in a pure and simple way, I do deny. For just as you might call a corpse a dead man but could not simply call it a man, so I would grant that the vicious are evil, but I cannot admit that they are, absolutely. Just as I call a person's corpse a dead person, and not a real person,

so I may call the vicious evil beings, but not beings in the full sense. For that which keeps its order and preserves its nature truly is. For that truly is which stands in its proper place and keeps its nature. But whatever falls away from this (that is, from nature) also gives up the being that is grounded in its nature. Whatever abandons nature has abandoned its being, which rested on that nature. The good is nature. Whatever renounces the good has renounced nature, in which every single thing subsists. Nature gives a thing the ability to subsist and to be. Without nature it is not. That is an argument from cause: nature is the cause of being.
THAT THE POWER OF THE WICKED IS RATHER WEAKNESS. "But," you will say, "the wicked have power." So you say of the wicked that they have power. I would not deny it. I do not deny that.

But this power of theirs comes not from strength but from weakness. Whatever power they have does not come from strength but from lack of strength. For they are able to do evil things, which they would not be able to do at all if they could have remained in the effective doing of good. They are able to do evil, which they could not do if they were able to remain steadfast in good deeds. This ability shows all the more clearly that they can do nothing. Such powers are plainly powerlessness. That is an argument from contraries: if good deeds come from strength, then evil deeds necessarily come from lack of strength. For if evil is nothing, as we concluded a little earlier, that is, as we drew together from the arguments,
then since the wicked can only do evil, it is clear that they can do nothing.

If it is so, as we said a while ago in our discussion, that evil is nothing, then it is plain that those who can only do evil can do nothing. We should understand collectio, conclusio, illatio and confectio as all meaning the same thing. "It is clear." "That is plain," I said.

[?] [THAT THE WICKED] CAN DO NOTHING; LIKEWISE THAT THOSE WHO CAN DO EVIL [CAN DO NOTHING], SINCE THE ALMIGHTY CANNOT DO IT. "And yet, so that you may understand what the force of this power is: a little earlier we established that nothing is more powerful than the highest good." "Now," she said, "so that you may understand what kind of power this is: I said just before that nothing is mightier than the highest good." "So it is," I said.

"So you did," I said. "But it cannot do evil," she said. "Now, it cannot do evil," she said. "By no means." "No, it cannot," I said. "Is there then anyone," she said, "who thinks that people can do all things?" "Is there anyone," she said, "who believes that people are able to do all things?"
"No one, unless he is insane." "No, not unless he is raving," I said. "And yet they can do evil?" "Can they do evil?" she said.
"I wish they could not," I said. "Would to God they could not," I said. "Since, then, the one who has power only for good can do all things,

But since those who are able to do all things cannot do evil [?], it is plain that those who can do evil are less able. Since he is almighty who can do only good, and those who can do only evil are not almighty, it follows that they are less able. Because he can do less than good, he can therefore do nothing. Since he is almighty who can do everything except evil, those who on the contrary can do everything except good can do nothing. This is an argument from contraries.
SINCE POWER IS TO BE SOUGHT, WHAT IS NOT TO BE SOUGHT IS NOT POWER. PROPOSITION. To this is added

what we have shown: that all power is to be counted among the things to be desired, and that all things to be desired are referred to the good, as to a kind of summit of their nature. To this also belongs what I said: that all power is among the things that are to be desired, and that everything that is to be desired is directed toward the good, as toward the head of its kind.
ASSUMPTION. But the ability to commit crime cannot be referred to the good. But the fact that one can do evil does not look toward the good.

CONCLUSION. Therefore it is not to be desired. So it is not to be desired either. This is a conditional syllogism. A conditional syllogism always has a double proposition, because there are two propositions in it. Of these two, one is used for the assumption and the other for the conclusion. So in this proposition there is one predication: all power is to be desired. The other is: all things to be desired are referred to the good. The assumption is made with the second: the ability to commit crimes is not referred to the good. The conclusion is made with the first: therefore it is not to be desired.
LIKEWISE. But all power is to be desired. Now surely all power is to be desired. It is clear, therefore, that the ability to do evil is not power.

From this it is clear that the ability of the wicked is not power. How is it clear? Because it is not to be desired. This again is a complete syllogism. One part is the premise: all power is to be desired. The other part is understood without being stated: but the power of the wicked is not to be desired. The inference is then: it is clear, therefore, that the ability of the wicked is not power. From all this the power of the good is clear, and the weakness of the wicked is beyond doubt. From all these arguments the power of the good becomes clear, and so does the certain powerlessness of the wicked. And it is clear that Plato's saying is true, that only the wise can do what they desire. And it is clear that the words of Plato are true, who said that only the wise can do
what they wish. But the wicked can indeed carry out what pleases them, yet they cannot achieve what they desire. And the wicked can do whatever their hearts want,

and yet they cannot bring it to completion. They persecute the good as they please, yet they never [?] them. For they do what pleases them, because they think that through the things they delight in they will gain the good they desire. They do what they want, because by doing what they lust after they expect to win the happiness they long for. But they do not gain it at all, since shameful deeds do not lead to blessedness. But they do not win it, because the wicked do not come to happiness.
THAT THOSE WHOM UNJUST MASTERS OPPRESS ARE NOT FREE. The kings whom you see sitting on the lofty height of the throne
gleaming in bright purple, hedged about with grim weapons,
threatening with fierce faces, panting with rage of heart.
If anyone should strip from these proud ones, that is, kings, the coverings of their vain adornment,
he will at once see that within, these lords bear tight chains.

Those overproud kings whom you now see sitting on a high throne, gleaming in their purple, surrounded by armed servants, threatening with fierce looks, panting with arrogance: whoever strips from them what adorns them outwardly, that is, whoever comes to know them inwardly, will see them, lords though they are, bound with chains like slaves. What are the chains? For on this side lust turns their hearts with greedy poisons.
on that side turbulent wrath, raising up waves,

lashes the mind; or sorrow wears down the captives, or slippery hope torments them. On one side desires assail them with poisonous greed; on the other side anger troubles them, rising up like a wave; or sadness torments them, or vain hope holds them fettered.
Therefore, when you see one head bearing so many tyrants,
it does not do what it itself wishes, oppressed by unjust masters.
When one man endures so many rulers, he does not do what he wants, because he is held in constraint by such unfit lords.

ON THE SURE REWARD OF THE GOOD. Do you see, then, in what filth wickedness wallows, and with what light goodness shines? Do you not now see in what mire the wicked are stuck, and in what beauty the good shine? In this it is plain that rewards are never lacking to the good, nor their punishments to crimes. Herein it is clear that the good never lack their reward, nor the wicked their punishment.
For of the things that are done, that for the sake of which each thing is done

may not unjustly be seen as the reward of that thing. It must rightly seem to us that the reward of all deeds lies in that for the sake of which they are done. Just as in the stadium the reward of running lies in the crown, for the sake of which one runs. Just as in a footrace the crown lies as the reward, for the sake of which one runs. What a stadium is we shall explain in the following chapter. But we have shown that happiness is that very good for the sake of which all things are done. Now I have shown that happiness is the one good for whose sake all things are done.
The good itself, therefore, is set before human actions

as a common reward. Therefore that same good is offered to the deeds of all people as a common reward. But this, that is, the reward, cannot be separated from the good. That same reward cannot [be separated] from the good. For he who lacks the good will no longer rightly be called good. Nor could anyone any longer be called good who were without the good. Therefore their rewards do not abandon upright ways. Therefore their reward never escapes the good. However much, then, the wicked may rage, the crown will yet not fall from the wise man, nor will it wither. Let the wicked rage as much as they like, the good do not lose their crown on that account, nor does it wither as those made of flowers did, which were customary in former times.
For another's wickedness does not pluck from upright souls their own glory. Nor does the wickedness of others ever take away from the good their honor.
If he rejoiced in something received from outside, another person, or even the one who had bestowed it, could take it away. If they rejoiced in the outward reward,

such as gold and silver are, then the one who gave it to them, or someone else, could snatch it from them. But since each person's own goodness confers it (that is, the reward), he will lose his reward only when he ceases to be good.
