This is the love common to all things. This is the love I am speaking of, which is common to all things. God himself is what they love, for he is the highest good (summum bonum), and they came from him.
And they seek again, that is, they desire, to be held by the end of the good. And so they long to be bound to the end of the good, which he is.
Because they could not last in any other way
unless, with their love turned back, they flowed back to the cause, that is, unless they joined themselves to that cause

which gave them being. For they could not exist in any other way unless they made their way back, with their love turned around, to the God who commanded them to come into being, who is the cause of them all.
THAT ALL FORTUNE IS GOOD. So do you see now what follows from all these things we have said?

"Do you not now perceive what necessarily follows from all these things?" "What then?" I said. "What, I said?" "That all fortune is entirely good," she said. "That both are good: good fortune and misfortune."
"And how can that be?" I said. "How can that be?" I said. "Pay attention," she said. "Listen to this," she said. "Since all fortune, whether pleasant or harsh,
is bestowed for the sake either of rewarding or exercising the good, or of punishing or correcting the wicked, all fortune is good, since it is established to be either just or useful."

"Since every kind of fortune, the pleasant and the toilsome alike, is permitted for this reason, that it may reward the good or test them, and that the wicked may pay for it or be improved, then it is necessarily good, being just or useful. This is an argument from the effect: from the effect it is seen what kind of thing the efficient cause is." "The reasoning is very true indeed," I said. "The argument is exceedingly true!" I said. "And if I consider the providence which you taught a little before, or fate, the opinion rests on firm strength." "And if I look at both, providence and fate, of which you spoke just now, then it has great force. For what else does God's providence or the disposition of fate do with all fortunes

but these four things: reward or punish, test or improve? And what can be more just, and at the same time more beneficial?" "But, if you please, let us count it among those things which you a little before showed to be beyond belief." "Now let us nevertheless put it, if it seems right to you, with the incredible things you spoke of before, such as this one: that wicked men who are punished are happier than those who go unpunished." "Why?" she said. "How so, then?" she said. "Why should I put it with those?"
"Because the common talk of men makes use of this, and indeed often: that some people's fortune is bad." "Because it is the people's talk," I said, "and often, that bad fortune befalls some."
"Do you wish, then," she said, "that we draw near for a little while to the talk of the common people,

so that we do not seem to have withdrawn too far, as it were, from the usage of humankind?" "Do you wish," she said, "that I come close to the people's talk, so that I do not separate myself too sharply from the everyday talk of men? Do you wish me to speak in a way more easily believed?" "As you please," I said. "As you wish," I said.
PREMISE. "Do you not, then, judge that what is beneficial is good?" "Do you not think," she said, "that what is useful is good?"
"So it is," I said. "That it is," I said.
PREMISE. "But that which exercises or corrects is beneficial?" "The fortune that tests or improves a man," she said, "is it not useful?" "I admit it," I said. "That I confess," I said.

CONCLUSION. "Therefore it is good." "Then it is good," she said. "Why not?" "How else?" I said. In this syllogism she has drawn close to the people's talk, for although it pursues the same argument as the argument before it, its words are nevertheless more credible to people
than those were. "But this fortune belongs to those who, either established in virtue, wage war against hardships, or, turning away from vices, take up the path of virtue."

"But such fortune," she said, "which tests or improves a man, belongs to one of two kinds of people: either to those who are virtuous and struggle against hardships, or to those who are now beginning to turn from vices to virtue." "I cannot deny it," I said. "That I can never deny," I said.

TO THE GOOD ALL FORTUNE IS GOOD, AND TO THE WICKED ALL FORTUNE IS BAD. But what of the pleasant fortune that is given to the good as a reward? But what, she said, of the pleasant fortune that comes to the good as a reward? Do the common people judge it to be bad? Do the people also say that it is bad? By no means; but just as it is,
so they also judge it to be the best.
No, I said; they call it good, as it is. What of the rest? But what, she said, of the other kind? Since it is harsh and restrains the wicked with just punishment, do the people think it good?

I mean the fortune that is harsh and punishes the wicked as justice requires: do the people consider it good? On the contrary, I said, they judge it the most wretched of all that can be imagined. They consider it, I said, the worst of everything one can know of. See, then, that by following the people's opinion we do not end up with something truly unbelievable. See now that by following the people's opinion we do not establish something too unbelievable. This is said by way of contrast, as if she said: see whether I should hold back, out of regard for the people's opinion, from saying what is unbelievable to them. What? I said. What is the unbelievable thing? I said.
From what has been granted, she said, it follows that for those who are in possession of virtue,
or advancing in it, or attaining it, every fortune whatever is good, but for those who remain in wickedness every fortune is the worst.

It truly follows of necessity, she said, from the earlier admissions, that every kind of fortune is good for those who are settled in virtue, or are striving toward it, or have at least attained it; but for those who hold fast to their wickedness, every kind of fortune is equally bad. That is true, I said, although no one would dare to admit it. That is true, I said, though no one dares to admit it, because it is so hard to believe.

WITH WHAT MIND ALL FORTUNE IS TO BE BORNE. Therefore, she said, a wise man ought not to take it badly whenever he is drawn into a struggle with fortune, just as it does not befit a brave man to be indignant whenever the noise of war has sounded. Therefore, she said, a wise man should not be troubled whenever he has to fight with fortune, just as it does not befit a bold warrior to resent it
when he hears the storm of battle. For to each of them the difficulty itself is the material: for the one, to spread his glory; for the other, to shape his wisdom.

The hardship itself gives both of them the opportunity: the one to make his glory famous, the other to make his wisdom perfect. It is from this that virtue gets its name: relying on its own strength, it is not overcome by adversity. Virtue is named from this: it is strong enough of itself and does not give way to adversity. For you who have been set on the path of advancing in virtue did not come here to melt away in delights and wither in pleasure. What are you thinking? You virtuous ones, you were not sent there to grow slack and idle in softness and pleasure.
You join a very fierce battle with every fortune.

You wage a fierce war with every fortune. So that neither sad fortune overwhelms you nor pleasant fortune corrupts you, hold the middle, that is, equanimity, with firm strength. Hold yourselves fast to equanimity, so that sorrowful fortune does not weigh you down and overcome you, and pleasant fortune does not corrupt your minds so far that you no longer know who you are. Whatever either stops below or goes beyond this middle shows contempt for happiness and has no reward for its labour. Whatever lets itself sink lower than equanimity, or climbs higher, loses happiness and goes without the reward.
For it lies in your own hands what kind of fortune you choose to shape for yourselves.

It is up to you what kind of fortune you wish to make for yourselves, and how evenly you wish to bear yourselves toward it. For every fortune that seems harsh punishes, unless it either trains or corrects. Whatever seems harsh does one of these things: it either toughens a person, or improves him, or punishes him.
ON THOSE WHO CONQUERED ADVERSITY BY VIRTUE. The avenging son of Atreus, having waged war for twice five years,
atoned for his brother's lost marriage-bed

with the ruins of Phrygia. Agamemnon, the son of Atreus, avenged the stolen wife of his brother Menelaus by destroying Troy, waging a ten-year siege. It is well known how Alexander Paris, the son of Priam, plundered Sparta, a city of Greece, took Helen, the wife of King Menelaus, while the king was away, and carried her home to Troy. It is also known how the Greeks went after them to take revenge and besieged Troy without stopping until they conquered it and won Helen back. He, that is, Agamemnon, while he wished to give sails, that is, winds, to the Greek fleet
and while he bought the winds, that is, appeased them, with blood, that is, his daughter's blood,
put off the father,

that is, stripped himself of the name of father, and the grieving priest, that is, Calchas, cut the wretched throat, that is, the breast, of the daughter. In this way Agamemnon became childless. Because he wanted to sail away quickly, he sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia to the winds, and Calchas pitifully slaughtered her as if she were a sacrificial animal. This showed how earnest he was: he did not even spare his daughter, so long as he could avenge his name.
The man of Ithaca wept for his lost companions,
whom savage Polyphemus, in his rage, swallowed into his monstrous belly.
But afterward, as the giant lay with blinded face, that is, countenance, in his vast cave,

Ulysses repaid his sad tears with joy. Ulysses mourned his companions, whom the giant Polyphemus furiously devoured in Sicily as Ulysses was returning from Troy. But he was compensated for his tears, because afterward the giant lay blind for a long time in his cave. Ulysses found him asleep and blinded him, and then he was consoled for his comrades, because he had avenged them.
His hard labours make Hercules famous. The many labours that Hercules overcame made him renowned.

He tamed the proud Centaurs. He subdued the Centaurs, who according to the fables were half man and half horse. He came to the place where they were playing in the water, and there he shot two of them.

He took a spoil from the savage lion. This was the lion the Greeks called the Nemean, after Nemea, a forest of the Argives. Hercules killed it at the will of King Aristeus. He took its hide and afterward wore it, claws and all, as a mark of glory.
He also shot down the birds with unerring arrows.

He also shot the birds that are called Harpies, and drove them out of the kingdom of King Alcinous, who had his seat in Achaia. From there they fled to the Strophades islands, where Aeneas found them. They were the fabled hounds of Jupiter, named from rapiendo ("seizing"), because Greek arpo means rapio ("I seize") in Latin. But Ovid calls them Stymphalides, from the river Stymphalus, beside which Hercules fought with them, however it may be said that the Argonauts drove them away. "He snatched the apples while the dragon looked on." While the dragon looked on, he took the golden apples that it guarded in the garden of the Hesperides islands, which lie out beyond Mount Atlas in the western ocean. The story that golden apples grow there has spread from one of those same islands, which is most fertile in every kind of produce. And because there is an estuary of the sea in it,

that is, an inlet of the sea, which shows the likeness of a dragon to those who see it from far off, people therefore say that a dragon lies there and guards the apples. An aestuarium is the water that comes in from the sea and floats on the shore. It is named from aestuando, just as stagnum ("pool") is named from stando ("standing"). So it has its name from aestuando, that is, from surging, because when the sea comes in, it surges, though it is still when the sea goes out. Aestus properly means the restlessness of the sea, which it has of itself by approaching and receding, that is, by going out and coming in. "His left hand weighed down with golden metal,"

that is, with the club, "he dragged Cerberus on a triple chain." And armed with a club, he dragged Cerberus out of hell on a threefold chain. Because of this it happened that when Cerberus came up here into the light of day, he became sick and spat out a foam, and from it grew aconite, the worst of herbs.
"The victor is said to have set out cruel fodder"

"for the savage four-horse team: their master." He gave the savage king Glaucus, once he had overcome him, to his own savage horses to eat. He did this because the king had earlier trained them to eat human flesh.
"The Hydra perished, its venom burned up." He destroyed the poisonous serpent, the Hydra, with fire.
"The river Achelous, disfigured on his brow,"
"plunged his shamed face into his banks."

The river Achelous, having been made hornless, hid his shamed head in the bank. Achelous changed himself into various shapes until he also became a bull and fought with Hercules. When Hercules struck off his horn and left his head maimed, he hid it afterward. All waters are horned because of the trees that stand around them. Whoever takes the trees away has made them hornless. Because Hercules also cleared the forest from the bank, he took the river's horns from it. "He laid Antaeus low on the Libyan sands." He also overcame the giant Antaeus, son of Earth and king of Libya. He could not overcome him by wrestling while Antaeus stood on the earth, because his mother Earth gave him strength. Then he lifted him up and strangled him in the air.
"Cacus satisfied the wrath of Evander." Cacus the thief, son of Vulcan, who stole Hercules' cattle,
cooled the anger of King Evander by his death. When Hercules slew him, he had done Evander a favour, for Cacus practised robbery in Evander's kingdom.
"The bristly boar flecked his shoulders with foam."

which the high sphere would press, that is, which it would bear down upon. The boar foamed onto his shoulders, with which he was to hold up heaven. It did that snorting at his head, because he carried it alive. His last labor, that is, in his last labor: he held up heaven with unbending neck. In his last victory he held up heaven with an unyielding neck. That was when Jove defended himself against the giants and wanted to hurl heaven down on them.
And in turn he earned heaven as the reward for his last labor. And as his reward he himself went to heaven, because he was the last to hold it up.
Go now, you brave ones.

where the lofty path of a great example leads. Now take him as your example, all you virtuous ones, and go where the way that goes on high leads you. Why do you sluggards bare your backs? The earth, once overcome, gives the stars. Why should you yield like cowards and turn your backs? Despise the earth; that gives you heaven.

TO WHICH PART OF PHILOSOPHY THE QUESTIONS OF THIS FOURTH BOOK, AND OF THE FIFTH BOOK STILL TO FOLLOW, BELONG. Just as the questions in the third book are moral ones, which show the happiness of the good, so are those here in the fourth book, which show us the misery of the wicked, and those that come after them, about providence and fate. But the ones still to come in the fifth book, about chance and free will, divide into two kinds. Chance belongs to providence, so that is a moral question. But whether providence and free will can exist together, which he has yet to ask Philosophy, belongs to theology, because it reveals the nature of God's simplicity. That is, it belongs to the kind of reasoning that deals with divine things. This reasoning,

because it is not human but divine, has a different name: it is called intellect. The understanding of divine things goes beyond human reason. That is why the questions she explained to us about the reward of the good and the wicked are supported with arguments and syllogisms. But the hidden power in God's providence, which she has yet to tell of, is divine, and so it will be grasped in a divine way. You may ask what God's disposition, which is in fate and in providence, has to do with morality, since morality gets its name from mores, that is, manners. Then you should know that God's disposition is called moral by analogy with human morality. How people behave

or how they ought to behave is called in Latin moralitas, the quality of manners. So the way God responds to that same behavior is also called morality: both here, by dealing out to each, as was said above, and hereafter, by rewarding. In the same way blessed Gregory teaches a moral lesson in his homily: God would not give a drop of water to the man who would not give the poor man a crumb of bread. That is why the Savior said: "With the same measure that you have measured, it shall be measured back to you." The proverb agrees with this: "Do evil, and do not expect better." What, then, is morality, except how things go, and ought to go, in human behavior, and how God's behavior answers to it in return? HERE ENDS THE FOURTH BOOK OF BOETHIUS.

HERE BEGINS THE FIFTH BOOK OF BOETHIUS. PHILOSOPHY IS CALLED BACK FROM THE DISCUSSION SHE HAD PROPOSED. She had spoken, that is, she had finished the preceding songs, which make the end of the fourth book. This she said. And she was turning the course of her speech to certain other matters to be treated and explained. To other matters, that is, than I wished. So she had turned to a different subject than I wanted. I wanted her to explain the incidental questions; she, however, wanted to finish the questions she had proposed. Here we must understand that the questions with which she wanted to heal his sick mind were the ones she had put before him in the first book. They are these: what man is; by what helms the world is ruled; what the end of things is; that wicked men are not to be believed powerful and happy;

and that the changes of fortune do not drift about without a ruler. She found him in grief over his misfortune. But when he had learned from her the reasoning behind these questions, I mean: that man is god by participation in God; that these are the helms of the world, that prosperity and adversity befall him; that all the reprobate are unhappy and powerless, because they cannot reach the good they strive toward; and that the changes of fortune he complained of are not unjust, because they come from the just God; then he began to take comfort. And from these questions he began to take up others that had sprung from them. She has explained some of these to him in the fourth book,

namely the causes of hidden things, the simplicity of providence, and the chain of fate. Those he now asks about are still to come: chance, divine predestination, and the freedom of the will. Then I said. Then I said to her: A right exhortation indeed. That is a right exhortation, namely what you say: "Go now, you brave, where the lofty road of great example leads." And entirely worthy of your authority. And it well befits your authority. But I find by experience what you said a while ago. I now become aware of what you said before: that the question of providence is entangled with many others. The discussion of providence is bound up with many others.

THE QUESTION OF CHANCE. For I ask whether you think chance is anything at all. I wonder whether you consider chance to be anything. And what you think it is. And what you take it to be. Then she said. Then she answered: I hasten to discharge the debt of my promise. I hasten to free myself from my promise. And to open to you the way by which you may be carried back to your homeland.

And to show you the way that will bring you home. The exile of your mind has caused you grief; I wish to hasten to set it back in its place, with other discourse [?]. But although these things are very useful to know. Although these questions are also useful to know, yet they turn somewhat aside from the path of what we set out to do. They still break away somewhat from the way I am travelling. And it is to be feared that, worn out by byways, you may not have strength enough to cover the right road. And I worry that you, having grown tired on byways, may afterwards be unable to travel the right way.
"Do not fear that at all," I said. "Do not fear that," I said. "For it will serve me as rest to learn the things in which I most delight."

For me it is rest, not toil, if I may learn what I long for. "At the same time, let there be no doubt about what follows." So that there can be no doubt about the rest of the discussion. "When every side of your argument has been established with undoubted credibility." That is, when the questions that came up along the side have first been brought to certainty. That is: so that the incidental questions which arise from the side, once they have first been untangled, may give credibility to the other things you have put forward. "Then she said: I will do as you wish." Now, she said, I will go along with your wishes. "And at once she began thus." With that she began as follows.

THAT CHANCE IS FALSELY SAID TO BE WITHOUT CAUSE. "If, she said, anyone defines chance as an event produced by random motion and by no connection of causes," if anyone calls chance an event that happened by accident and without anything causing it, "I affirm that chance is nothing at all." then I say boldly that chance is nothing. "And I judge it to be an entirely empty word, apart from signifying an underlying thing." And I call it a bare name without any meaning. Cause is always connected to the event. Therefore, when people say "by random motion" and "without cause" or "without connection of causes", it all comes to the same thing. All of it means: by accident, at random, without need, without origin,

without source, without cause, without reason. "Random motion" can also be called self-moving or self-raising. I mean it would be as if something raised itself up by itself and came into being by itself. But what is that? We can say it, but we never find it at all. Temeritas (rashness) is thoughtlessness, and heedlessness, and hasty alarm, and disorderliness, recklessness, lack of discernment, wrongness. Temerarius, that is, headlong of mind, is the one who does not care what he does, and who acts without counsel on whatever occurs to him in the moment.

Such a person we call a rash man [?]. Temeritas is derived from temnendo (despising) by syncope, as if it were temneritas. "For what place can there be for any rashness, when God holds all things together in order?" Where can there be what people call "by accident" and "at random" and "without order", when God compels all things into order? "For it is a true saying that nothing comes into being from nothing." What people say is entirely true, that nothing comes from nothing. "Which none of the ancients ever contradicted." All our forebears affirmed this. "Although they did not say this of the operating principle," though they did not say it of the Beginning, who makes all things out of nothing, "but of the material subject." but of things that have seed. Those things have seed which have a seed

and cannot come into being without it, such as trees and plants and all living creatures. These are called subjects, because they are subject to their accidents. The four elements are the seed of all of them and their matter. "But they (that is, the ancients) laid this down as a kind of foundation for all their reasonings about nature." And they laid down and showed this as the foundation of all the arguments and all the answers that they gave about nature. This kind of expression is called hypallage, where he says "foundation of reasonings" instead of "reasoning of the foundation". The sure reasoning at the foundation of all natures is this: that they said nothing comes into being from nothing.

Natures such as trees and plants, and all bodies: they do not come into being suddenly [out of nothing]. They have some matter from which they come into being; he calls that the foundation (fundamentum). And if anything happens to them, there is some cause of it, and that too is a foundation. There is always some reason, hidden or plain, for what their foundation is, where they come from, or where anything that happens to them comes from. But if something should arise from no causes at all, it would seem to have arisen from nothing. But if anything comes into being without an origin, it has come from nothing. And if this cannot happen, then chance cannot be the kind of thing we defined a little earlier. If that cannot be, then chance cannot be such as we said before either; I mean, that it is an event produced

by random motion. "What then?" I said. How then did I speak? "Is there nothing that could rightly be called either chance or fortuitous?" Can there be nothing that should rightly be called chance (casus) or the fortuitous (fortuitum)? "Or is there something these words fit, even though it is hidden from the common people?" Is there anything these names belong to, even though people do not recognize it?

WHAT CHANCE IS. "My Aristotle," she said, "defined it in the Physics, with a brief argument and one close to the truth." My friend, she said, Aristotle said it in his book the Physics, briefly and convincingly.

"In what way?" I said. How, I said, did he say it? "Whenever," he says, "something is done for the sake of some purpose," when someone, she said, does something somewhere for the sake of something, "and something other than what was intended comes about from certain causes, that is called chance." And when, from some source, something happens other than what one did it for,
that is called chance (casus). "As if someone digging the ground in order to cultivate a field were to find a mass of buried gold." It is like this:

if anyone, breaking up the earth for work in the field, finds a hoard of gold that was buried there long ago. "This is therefore believed to have happened by chance." People say it happened unexpectedly. "But it does not come from nothing." Yet it is not without cause; it happened from some source. "For it has its own causes." It has its own origins. "Their unforeseen and unexpected coming together seems to have produced chance." Their courses, coming together quietly and unexpectedly, produce the event.
"For if the cultivator of the field had not dug the ground,"

For if the farmer had not gone to the field there, "if the one who hid it had not buried his money in that place," and if the one who hid it had not buried his treasure there, "the gold would not have been found." Then it would not have been found there. "These, therefore, are the causes of the fortuitous gain," these are what produced the unexpected good fortune, "which arises from causes that meet and flow together," which came to him there from two things running together, that is, to produce a third, "not from the intention of the one acting." Neither of the two people involved intended it.
"For neither the one who buried the gold nor the one who worked the field

…intended that this money should be found. For neither the man who buried the gold nor the man who ploughed the field had any thought that it would be found there. But, as I said, it came together and coincided that this man dug where that man buried. Rather, as I said: where the one buried, the other dug there; these ran together and fell together. The one could not have brought about the event without the other. We may therefore define chance as
an unexpected event. Now I must say that chance is what happens unexpectedly. From causes flowing together in these things,

namely in causes, which are done for some purpose. From things that fall together, which people do for the sake of something. But that order which descends from the fountain of providence arranges all things in their places and times. But the order, namely the order of fate, which comes from God's providence, arranges all things one by one in their place and in their time. Proceeding by an inevitable connection. Coming with a firm bond. It makes the causes run together and flow together. It makes the causes of chance events fall and run together and hold together. Providence knows things all together; fate unfolds them one by one. For where one man had earlier buried, fate joined to that the fact that another later dug there; to those two the third, the finding, was joined by necessity. When God willed those two things to happen, the third happened from them by necessity.

LIKEWISE, A DEMONSTRATION OF CHANCE FROM THE MEETING OF RIVERS. The Tigris and the Euphrates spring from one source among the crags of the Achaemenian rock. On the mountains of Armenia the Tigris and the Euphrates spring up together. Where the fleeing battle,
that is, the fleeing fighter, fixes his turned-back arrows in the breasts of his pursuers.
There the fighters, while fleeing, shoot behind them at those who pursue them.
And soon, their waters parted, they separate. And they at once part from each other in far-apart courses.
If they should come together and be called back again into one course — (the voice is held in suspense here). If after that they flow together and come into one channel,
so that what the wave of each stream carries would flow together,

And here: thus, so that what each water carries would flow together. Ships would meet, and trunks torn up by the river. And here: I mean the ships, and the tree trunks torn out of the earth by the river.

And the mingled water would entangle chance modes, that is, orders; namely, this is called chance. And the mingled water entangles the unexpected orders. These are orders: that water always runs after water. If that happens unexpectedly, the occurrence is called chance.
Yet these wandering chances are governed by the very slopes of the land

and by the downward-flowing order of the falling stream. These same occurrences, I mean those of the confluence, are caused by the slopes and by the river's course, which always sinks downward. If there were no valley, and the water did not hasten there, they would not come together. So chance submits to the reins,
though it seems to drift with loosened reins.

So chance goes under constraint, though it seems to you to go unconstrained. And it proceeds by its own law. And it does not go without law. The causes that make chance constrain it; they set a law for it. Therefore chance, accident and unexpected event are what the causes make, whether open or hidden.
WHETHER THE HUMAN WILL IS CONSTRAINED BY FATE.
I see it, I said. I understand it well. And I agree that it is so, as you say.

And I see that it is so, as you say. But is there no freedom of our will in this series of causes that cohere with one another? Is there now no self-determination of our will in this chain of causes that hold together? Or does the chain of fate constrain even the motions of human minds? Does fate also compel human thoughts, as it does other events?
"There is," she said, "free will." "There is," she said. "Nor could there be any rational nature that did not also have freedom of will.
No creature has reason without free will. The angels in heaven and men on earth have both.

THAT JUDGMENT COMES FROM REASON, AND CHOICE FROM FREEDOM. For whatever can naturally use reason has judgment. One who has been granted understanding and mind has also been granted choice, by which he may discern each thing. With it he distinguishes each thing, whether it ought to be done or not. In these two he is unconstrained. This unconstrainedness is called freedom. Reason teaches him what he ought to do; freedom lets him do whichever he wishes. By itself, therefore, it distinguishes what is to be shunned and what is to be desired. He knows of himself what he should shun
or love. Reason teaches him that. But what someone judges to be desirable, he seeks; he flees

what he judges ought to be shunned. What he thinks is good, he wills; what he thinks is evil, he shuns. Free will allows him this. Therefore those who have reason also have the freedom of willing and not willing. Hence those who have been granted knowledge of evil and good have been granted the power of choice. But I do not hold, that is, I do not acknowledge, that this freedom is equal in all. I say, however, that it is not equal
in all who have it. For clear-sighted judgment, uncorrupted will, and effective power to obtain what they desire are present to the higher, divine substances.

For the angels have been granted true knowledge, right will, and effective power to carry out their will. God gave these three things as a reward to the good angels after the fall of the evil ones, who turned their free will to evil while they still had it. Now they do not have it. Even though they recognize what is good to do, they do not want to do it, nor can they. Man, however, before his transgression, had power over both, understanding and will. Through the transgression both were so confused that, when he chooses, he often takes a lie for the truth, and when he wills, he wills evil in place of good. Moreover, his will does not succeed, even when he wills well, unless the grace of God brings it about.
HE SPEAKS FROM THE OPINION OF THE PHILOSOPHERS. But human souls must be freer when they keep themselves in the contemplation of the divine mind.

Therefore human souls are necessarily freer while they have the sight of God in heaven. There neither error oppresses them, neither of judging nor of choosing. There they know, before they came here, what is good for them; and that they also want. But they are less free when they slip down into bodies. Coming here into bodies, they become unfree. And less free still when they are bound by earthly limbs. And also unfree when they take up a dwelling [in the body] and are fastened to the earthly limbs. But the most extreme servitude is when, given over to vices, they have fallen from the possession of their own reason. That is the most extreme servitude, when they, given over to sins, depart from their wisdom.
For when they have cast down their eyes (that is, of the mind) from the light of the highest truth to lower and darker things. Thus they become enslaved.

When they let their mind sink down from what is above to what is below. Soon they are darkened by the cloud of ignorance. Then they at once become ignorant. They are troubled by pernicious affections. They become fettered by harmful desires. By approaching and consenting to these. By yielding to them and following them. They assist the servitude which they have brought upon themselves. They strengthen the servitude which they let come upon themselves. And they are in a certain way captives through their own freedom. And then they are exiled and estranged from their freedom.
Which, nevertheless, that gaze of providence beholds, foreseeing all things from eternity.

This the foreseeing eye nevertheless always beholds, foreknowing all things. And it disposes each of the things predestined according to their merits, that is, whom he predestined, these he also rewards. And the things foreordained it shapes according to their deserts. [Greek:] 'Seeing all things and hearing all things.' That eye sees all and knows all.
HOW MUCH MORE PENETRATING THE GAZE OF GOD IS THAN THE RAY OF THE SUN. Homer of the honey-sweet mouth
sings of Phoebus as bright with pure light.
Homer, sweetly speaking, calls the sun bright
and clear. Which nevertheless is not able to break through all the inner parts of the earth
or of the sea
with the weak light of its rays. Which nevertheless cannot shine through the earth and the sea, because of the weakness of its beams.
Not so the founder of the great world. God is not so powerless.
To him, beholding all things from on high,
the earth does not resist with any mass. Against his eyes, which look over all things, no thickness of the earth stands.
Night with its black clouds does not obstruct him. Nor does any darkness of the night.
He discerns in a single stroke of the mind what things are, what have been, and what are to come. In a single glance he beholds what was before and what is now
and what is yet to come. Him you could call the true sun, because he alone looks upon all things.
Him you may call the true sun! because he alone beholds all things.
QUESTION: SINCE WHAT IS FORESEEN MUST NECESSARILY HAPPEN, HOW DOES FREE WILL STAND? Then I said: Then I answered her.
Behold, I am again confounded by a more difficult uncertainty. Now I am stuck in even greater doubt.
She said: What is this? Which is that doubt? For I already guess by what things you are troubled.

I can well guess, she said, what troubles you. I said: They seem very much to oppose and fight against each other. It seems to me, I said, that these two struggle and are against one another: that God foreknows all things, and that there is any free choice of will.

That God knows everything beforehand, and yet it rests in man's will. For if God foresees all things and cannot be deceived in any way, then what providence has foreseen as future must necessarily come about. For if God knows everything beforehand, and his knowledge cannot deceive him, then what he knows to be coming must necessarily happen.
That is true. Therefore, if he foreknows from eternity not only the deeds of men but also their plans and wills, there will be no freedom of choice.

This is false. Therefore, if he always knows beforehand not only people's deeds but also their will, then free will is gone. For no other deed and no will of any kind can exist except what divine providence, which cannot be deceived, has foreseen. For nothing can happen in deed or in will that God's eye does not see, and no one can deceive it. That is true. For if they can be turned aside in a way other than they were foreseen,

there will no longer be firm foreknowledge of the future, but rather uncertain opinion, and I judge it wicked to believe this of God. If any of them can turn aside, then it cannot be called certain knowledge, but only uncertain supposition, and no one may accuse God of that.

THE ARGUMENT BY WHICH SOME THINK THEY SOLVE THE QUESTION IS REFUTED. For I do not approve of the reasoning by which some believe they can untie this knot of the question. Nor do I praise the argument with which some think they have answered this difficulty. For they say
that something will not come about because providence has foreseen that it will be, but, they say, the reverse: because something is going to be,

it cannot be hidden from divine providence. They say: it does not happen because God foresees it, but because it happens, therefore he foresees it. And in this way they think this necessity slips back to the opposite side. And so they think this necessity of future events turns back the other way. For, they say, it is not necessary that the things foreseen should happen, but it is necessary that the things that will be should be foreseen. They do not think that what God foresees happens of necessity, but that what is to happen is of necessity foreseen. By this reversal they think that the event causes the foresight, not that the foresight causes the event. As if the effort were about which is the cause of this matter,
whether foreknowledge is the necessity of future things, or future things are the necessity of providence.

As if I were struggling over which of the two is the cause of the other: whether foresight is the necessitating cause of future things, or future things are the necessitating cause of foresight. And as if we were not striving to show that the coming about of foreknown things is necessary, however the order of causes may stand. And as if it were not rather my task to show that the coming about of the things foreknown is necessary, whatever the order of the causes may be; that is, because it always seems to me that this necessity does away with free will.
Even if foreknowledge does not seem to impose on future things the necessity of coming about. Even though foresight does not lay necessity on future things.

The argument of those who are in error is shown by another line of reasoning. TAKEN FROM ARISTOTLE'S CATEGORIES. For if someone is sitting, the opinion that supposes he is sitting must be true; and conversely, if the opinion about someone that he is sitting is true,

he must be sitting. What they think is like this: if anyone believes that a person who is sitting is sitting, the belief does not deceive him. If the belief does not deceive him, then he is sitting. There is therefore necessity in both: in the one, necessity of sitting; in the other, necessity of truth. Both are necessary: both the sitting and the freedom from deception.

But no one sits because the opinion is true. A true belief does not make anyone sit. Rather, the opinion is true because someone's sitting came first. Rather, the sitting that comes first makes the belief true.
So, although the cause of the truth comes from one side, there is still a necessity common to both. So it happens that the cause of the truth is on one side only, but the necessity is on both sides.
It is clear that one may reason in the same way about providence and future things.

Such is the argument about God's foresight and about future things, that is, as those who err in this matter have understood it. For even if things are foreseen because they are going to happen, they do not come about because they are foreseen. For although God sees things beforehand because they are going to happen, as they think, still they do not happen because he foresees them. Nevertheless it is necessary either that future things be foreseen by God or that things foreseen come to pass. Now both are necessary: both that God foresees future things and that foreseen things happen. So here too, in the same way, the cause is on one side, as they think, while the necessity is on both sides.
This alone is enough to destroy freedom of the will. In that point this is enough to destroy free will, because necessity takes away the power to choose.

THE FALSE NOTION OF FOREKNOWLEDGE IS RIDICULED. But how backward it is to say that the outcome of temporal things is the cause of eternal foreknowledge! How utterly perverse it is for anyone to say that these temporal events are the cause of God's eternal knowledge. But what else is it to think

that God foresees future things because they are going to happen, than to suppose that things which happened long ago are the cause of that highest providence? What else is it? Whoever wants to believe that God knows future things because they are going to happen, of him I say that he believes events are the cause of God's knowledge.

IT IS PROPOSED AGAIN THAT FOREKNOWLEDGE CANNOT BE AVOIDED; OTHERWISE IT WOULD RATHER BE OPINION. To this must be added: this too must be added to it: just as, when I know that something is, it must necessarily be, so, when I know that something will be, it must necessarily be going to be. Just as it is necessarily so if I know something in the present, so too what I know as future necessarily happens afterwards. So it comes about
that the outcome of a foreknown thing cannot be avoided. So it always happens that a thing known beforehand cannot fail to take place.
Finally, if anyone should judge something to be otherwise than it actually is: but if anyone judges the thing otherwise,
than it is. That is not only not knowledge, but it is false opinion, far different from the truth of knowledge.

That is not only a lack of knowledge, but a false supposition, far removed from the truth of knowledge. Therefore, if anything is going to happen in such a way that its outcome is not certain and necessary: so, if anything is future in such a way that its coming is not certain and not necessary, how can it be foreknown that it will happen? How can anyone know beforehand that it is to come?
For just as knowledge itself is unmixed with falsehood, so that which is conceived by it cannot be otherwise than as it is conceived.

Therefore that does not come about, because just as knowledge does not mix with lies, so whatever it holds in its grasp cannot turn out otherwise than as it is held in its grasp. In knowledge the events lie comprehended; just as they lie there, so they necessarily come to pass. For this is the reason why knowledge lacks falsehood: that each thing must necessarily be such as knowledge comprehends it to be. Therefore knowledge is without lies, because each thing must necessarily be as knowledge has found that it is. What then? What now?
In what way does God foreknow these uncertain future things? The things that are uncertain: in what way does God know them beforehand?
For if he judges that things will inevitably happen

which it is also possible may not happen, he is deceived. If he supposes that future things cannot fail to happen when they nevertheless can fail to happen, then the supposition deceives him. It is wicked not only to think this, but even to say it aloud. It is wicked to say, not merely to think. But if, just as they are,
he determines that they will be in the future in such a way that he knows equally that they can either happen

or not happen. But if he determines them to be future just as they are, I mean that he knows them equally able to happen and not to happen: what kind of foreknowledge is this, which grasps nothing certain and nothing stable? What knowledge is that, which holds nothing certain and nothing stable within it? Or how is this different from that ridiculous prophecy of Tiresias: "Whatever I say will either be or not be"? Or how much more certain is that than the ridiculous prophecy of the Sibyl, the priestess of Apollo, when she said: "What I say is either true or false"?
For in what would divine providence surpass human opinion if, like men, it judges uncertain things

whose outcome is uncertain? How then does God's wisdom surpass men's supposition, if he doubts doubtful things just as they do? But if with him, the most certain source of all things, nothing can be uncertain: but if with him, the source of all things, nothing is doubtful, then the outcome of those things which he has firmly foreknown as future is certain. Then the things which he certainly knows to be future also happen without doubt.

Therefore there is no freedom in human counsels and actions, which the divine mind, foreseeing all things, binds and constrains to one outcome. Therefore man has no power over his deeds, good or evil, since God, who foreknows everything, compels him to that one outcome. That is a false conclusion.

IF FREE WILL TOO IS TAKEN AWAY BY THE NECESSITY OF FUTURE THINGS, THE WHOLE ORDER OF HUMAN LIFE IS OVERTURNED. Once this is accepted, it is clear how great a ruin of human affairs follows. If that is so, then there is no doubt how completely human affairs will fall to ruin.
For rewards and punishments are set before

the good and the wicked in vain. Then reward and penalty are promised in vain to the good and the wicked alike. No free and voluntary movement of their minds has deserved them. Since their unfree and not self-governing will can deserve neither of these. And then the thing that now seems most just will seem the most unjust of all. And then the thing that is now most just becomes the most unjust of all things. That is, that the wicked are punished or the good are rewarded. I mean rewarding the good and paying back the wicked.

Their own will does not send them to either. Their will does not lead them to it. Instead the necessity of what is to come compels them. Instead the necessity of the future forces them. Therefore neither vices nor virtues will be anything at all,
but rather a mixed and undistinguished confusion of all merits.

Then there are no vices and no virtues, but an equal and undivided mixture of all deserts. And nothing more wicked than this can be imagined: since the whole order of things is derived from providence, And this is the most dangerous of all things to take into one's thoughts: since providence orders all future things, and nothing is left to human counsels, And as long as nothing at all depends on human will, it follows that even our vices are traced back to the author of all good things.

Then there is no other course except that our sins are smeared onto God, who gives all good. Therefore there is no reason either to hope for anything or to pray for anything. No one can give any account of hope or of entreaty, or say what either is for! For what should anyone hope for, or even pray to avert, when an unbending chain of events links together everything that might be wished for? What should one hope for or entreat, when the unturnable straight course, that is, of fate, binds all desirable things together indissolubly, like a chain? If all things are held fast in their order as they were appointed, then whatever is to come to each person comes to him without entreaty.
Therefore that one and only exchange will be taken away, namely the exchange between God and men, of hoping and praying.

If it goes this way, then the only exchange between God and men is blocked, and so is the bargain that rests entirely on hope and on entreaties. For by the price of just humility, namely the humility that is in prayers, we earn the priceless return of divine grace. For with the worth of right humility, which is what entreaties are, we buy from him the precious payment of his grace. We cannot carry on any other trade with him at all. This is the only way in which men seem able to speak with God, That is the one way in which people can converse with God. and, by the very act of supplication, to be joined to that inaccessible light, even before they obtain what they ask. And by praying they draw near to the invisible light, even before they obtain anything.
And if, once the necessity of future things is accepted, these are believed to have no power,

If now, because of the necessity imposed on future things, hope is to avail nothing, what will there be by which we can be joined to that highest ruler of things and hold fast to him? By what thing, then, can we hold ourselves to God, the lord of all things?
Therefore the human race, severed and disjoined, will necessarily fall away from its source, as you sang a little before. So then must

the human race, as you sang in the middle of those verses "if you would [behold] the laws of the high Thunderer," crack apart like clay [?], broken off and separated from the true source from which it came.

WHAT HOLDS HIM BACK FROM UNDERSTANDING THIS QUESTION. HE HIMSELF INVESTIGATES. What discordant cause has dissolved the bonds of things? What discord disturbs the joining of two things, namely of God and of man, or of foreknowledge and free will?
O God, who has set such great wars between two truths? What god has given such strife to two truths? What things are truer than they are?
So that the things which stand firm singly, each on its own,

refuse to be yoked together when joined? That the things which exist separately, each by itself, will not go together? What necessity can separate God's providence and man's free will, so that they are not together in every deed of man?
Or is there no discord between truths? Or is there no discord among true things? The true and the false flee each other; two truths love each other.
And do certain things always hold together with one another? And the certain things always hold together.
that is, the things that are each certain in themselves? But the mind, that is, the soul, overwhelmed by the blind members, cannot know the fine bonds of things
by the fire of its smothered light.

But the fault is not theirs; rather, the human soul, because of its dullness, cannot know their hidden bonds, which you, however, know, Philosophy, and which I wish to learn from you. That is as if he said: Free will is entirely certain to us, because it is evident in the deeds of men. God's providence is equally certain in the other creatures, which do not have free will. But in man's deeds the two cannot exist together. Or if they can, then the reason how that may be is very hidden. That reason is hard for him to work out "by the fire of smothered light," that is, by the keenness of a weighed-down mind, with the confused understanding of the mind. The body makes the soul lose power over its understanding, which it had before it came to the body. It always strives toward it, but it succeeds poorly.
But why does it burn with such great love
to find the hidden signs of truth? Why then is it so urgent for it to discover the hidden word-signs of truth? Does it know
what it anxiously longs to know? Does it know what it wants to know?
But who labors to know what is already known? But who would ask about something
that he knows? But if it does not know, what does it blindly seek? And if it is so blind that it does not know it, what then does it want?
For who would desire anything without knowing it? Who is there who would want what he does not know?
Or who could pursue things unknown?
or where would he find it?

Or who can seek what he neither knows nor recognizes? Or how could he succeed in discovering it? Who, being ignorant, could recognize the form once it was found? And who can recognize what is unknown to him, even when he finds it?
Or when it, namely the soul, beheld the high mind, that is, God,
did it know the whole and the particulars equally? Or should we believe that it knew both, the particular things and the whole together, for as long as it looked upon God?
Now, hidden by the cloud of the bodily limbs,
it has not wholly forgotten itself. Now that it is truly darkened in the limbs, it still has some of it and has not forgotten everything. And it holds on to the whole,
losing the particulars. It knows the main point, but it does not know the details. No one has so good a memory that he remembers all the details as well as he remembers the main point.
Therefore whoever seeks the truth
is in neither state. Whoever asks after the truth, as I am doing now in this question, is in neither state. For he does not know [m ?]
and yet he is not wholly ignorant of everything. He neither knows all of it nor is ignorant of all of it.
But the whole, which he keeps and remembers,
he consults. He investigates the main point that he holds in his memory, going back over things seen on high.

He thinks deeply about what he saw, so that he can add the forgotten parts to the things he has kept, and through the things he remembers reach the things he has forgotten. Consider someone who has learned a book thoroughly and now remembers only the outline [?] of its summary, but turns to that summary often, so that from it he also recalls the rest. Cicero teaches us what a summary is in his Rhetoric, where he says: "The sum of the deed is: he committed homicide. The particulars, however, are what was done before the act, what after the act, what in the act itself, or around the act." If someone says to us, "Must the things that are foreseen necessarily come to pass?", we say: "Necessarily."

If he then says, "And will free will stand?", we say: "It will stand." He also says: "How will something be free that is necessary? Necessity and freedom cannot belong to one and the same thing. Or if they can, by what bonds are things that oppose each other tied together?" What do we say then? If those bonds are unknown to us, we cannot give a complete answer to this question. In that case we know only the whole, and we do not know the particulars. We shall learn the particulars hereafter from Philosophy herself.
FIRST RESPONSE.

THAT UNDERSTANDING, NOT REASON, MAKES THEOLOGIANS. Then she said, that is, then she answered me: "This is the old complaint about providence." This is the old complaint about God's providence, that it hinders free will. "It was vigorously argued by Marcus Tullius when he divided divination into its kinds." Cicero treated it at length when he divided prophecy into three parts: haruspicy, lightning-divination, and augury from birds. Haruspicy was taken from the livers of sacrificial animals, lightning-divination from flashes of lightning, and augury from the songs of birds. "And it is a matter that you yourself have long and thoroughly investigated." It is a thing that you, which means by you, have searched into very carefully.
But until now it has by no means been resolved carefully and firmly enough.

…by any of you. But it has never yet been truly or certainly explained by any of you. The cause of this darkness is this. That the motion, i.e., the effort, of human reason cannot be brought near to the simplicity of divine foreknowledge. That a person's reason, however hard it strives for it, cannot reach the simplicity of God's foreknowledge. If it could in any way be conceived, namely at least by the intellect, since it cannot be by reason. If anyone can know it by rising above reason, nothing doubtful will remain. For that person there is no doubt about this question. God's foreknowledge is simple, for he knows all things

and knows them all at once, as present. He does not remember them behind him or think ahead to them before him. Whoever recognizes this has no doubt that the deeds of free will are also necessarily in his knowledge, but not in foreknowledge. They can exist together in the same way that our knowledge exists together with the deeds of people, which are free. How does our knowing their deeds hinder their freedom? I will try at last to make this plain and resolve it in this way, if I first weigh the things that trouble you. I will then try to reveal and explain that simplicity to you, once I have first set you right and examined what weighs on you and makes you doubt free will.

WHY SHE DOES NOT ACCEPT THE ARGUMENT BY WHICH OTHERS THINK THEY SOLVE THE QUESTION. For I ask why you think less effective that argument of those who solve it. Now I ask you why you do not think useful the argument of those who solve the question, that is, as they think they do. It holds that the freedom of choice is in no way hindered by foreknowledge. That argument holds, i.e., contends, that free will is not hindered by foreknowledge. Because it judges that foreknowledge is not a cause of necessity for future things. Because it does not impose necessity on future things, i.e., on the things to come, i.e., in their opinion. Here let us remember that he did not find fault with this opinion earlier, nor should he have, for it is correct. What he found fault with was their saying that the outcome of future things was the cause of God's foreknowledge.
For do you draw the argument for the necessity of future things from anywhere else?

From what else do you also infer that future things must happen by necessity? Except that the things that are foreknown cannot fail to happen? Except that the things that are foreknown cannot fail to come about? Here again we must consider how true that argument is. Everyone who wrestles with this question gets stuck here. What God foresees, they say, cannot fail to happen. That is true. What cannot fail to happen happens by necessity. That is also true. If these two truths are understood without a distinction, the conclusion follows that there is no free will. She teaches us that distinction later on. She teaches us that people's deeds can indeed fail to happen.

…insofar as it depends on their own nature. On that side there is no necessity in them at all, and yet, with God looking on them, they cannot fail to happen. It is the same when we look on and see a man sitting: his sitting cannot then be left undone, even though, as far as he was concerned, it could well have been left undone, because he could have refrained from it. From this comes the question whether his sitting gives us and God knowledge of his sitting. It is answered thus: it gives that knowledge to us when it happens, not before. But God's knowledge does not wait for the event. To him it is present before it happens, and this presence makes him know it. So the solution of this question is this: what God foresees is necessary, because he looks upon it.
In the same way it is necessary that when we see someone doing something, he is doing it, even though the doer does not do it of necessity.

BECAUSE PROVIDENCE DOES NOT COMPEL FUTURE THINGS, FREEDOM THEREFORE STANDS. If, then, foreknowledge adds no necessity to future things, as you yourself admitted a little earlier… If foreknowledge imposes no necessity on future things, as you also fully admitted before… What is it that compels the voluntary outcomes of things toward a fixed result? By what, then, are the self-determined courses of human deeds forced toward a certain outcome? Because they are free of compulsion, free will therefore stands. For let us suppose, for the sake of argument (that is, as an example), that there is no foreknowledge, so that you may see what follows. Now let us just say, for the sake of discussion, that foreknowledge does not exist, so that you may see how things then turn out.

Are the things that come from free choice then compelled into necessity, as far as this reasoning goes? Does any necessity then compel, on that account, the deeds that come from free will? By no means. It does not. Let us suppose again that it exists. Now let us say again that it does exist, but that it imposes no necessity on things. And yet it puts no necessity on the deeds.
The same freedom of will, I think, will remain whole and unrestricted. Even then, I think, that same free will still stands firm.

EVEN IF PROVIDENCE IS A SIGN OF FUTURE THINGS, IT IS NOT THEIR CAUSE. But you will say… Now you will say again: Even though foreknowledge is not a necessity that compels future things to happen… Even if foreknowledge is no compulsion on future things, it is still a sign that they will necessarily come about. It is still a sign that they must come about of necessity.

In this way, then, it would be established that the outcomes of future things are necessary, even if there had been no foreknowledge. It would then be just as certain that future things must necessarily happen, even if the foreknowledge of them did not exist.
For every sign shows only what the thing it signifies is; it does not bring that thing about. A sign shows only what the thing is that it is a sign of.

It does not bring that thing about, just as the red sky in the morning signals a storm and yet does not cause it. Therefore you must first prove that nothing happens except by necessity. You must first show us that all things happen of necessity, so that it may appear that foreknowledge is a sign of this necessity. Then we may believe that foreknowledge is a sign of that necessity. Otherwise, if there is no such necessity… But if it does not exist (that is, necessity)…
Not even that will be able to be a sign of a thing which does not exist.

So foreknowledge cannot then be their sign. But now it is established. We know well. That a proof supported by firm reasoning. The sure confirmation of any thing. Is not to be drawn from signs. Is not to be taken from a sign, as you do. Nor from arguments sought from outside. Nor from remote reasonings. As you want to infer necessity from remote signs. But from fitting and necessary causes. But from things that lead to it and that bring about necessity. Thus this argument is from fitting and necessary causes: The first man, because he had no father or mother, was not born. Or this: Because you have today neither eaten

nor drunk, you are fasting. But this, on the other hand, is taken from outside: Our fathers ate sour grapes, and the teeth of the sons are set on edge. For the parents are one set of people, and the sons are another. But to be fasting is nothing other than not to have eaten and not to have drunk; and to be unborn is nothing other than not to have a father or mother.

THINGS FORESEEN MUST NECESSARILY HAPPEN; YET THERE IS NO NECESSITY IN THEM THEMSELVES. But how can it be that those things do not come about which are foreseen as future? But how can it be that those things do not happen which God knows to be future? As if indeed we believed that those things will not come about which the providence of God foreknows to be future! As if I doubted that those things will happen which God foresees.

But should we not rather judge this: And should one not rather maintain this: Although they come about, Though they happen, Yet they have nothing of necessity by their own nature that they should come about. That they in themselves have no necessity by which they happen.
Which you may easily weigh from this.

Which you can easily perceive from this. For we behold many things placed before our eyes while they are being done. We see plenty of things that are before our eyes while someone is doing them. Such as the things charioteers are seen to do in guiding and turning their four-horse chariots. Such as what we see the chariot-drivers do, turning, namely in the chariot race, and also giving the chariots free rein as they will. And other things of this kind. And other works besides.
Does any necessity, then, compel any of those things to be done in this way?

Does any necessity compel any of them to it, against a man's will? By no means. It does not. For the working of skill would be in vain. One would be able to do it to no purpose. If all things moved under compulsion. If they went thus against a man's will. Therefore those things which lack necessity while they are being done, Those which are without necessity in the doing,
These same were future without necessity

before they happen. They too are, before they come to be, future without necessity. Wherefore there are certain things that are going to come about whose outcome is free from all necessity. From this it is clear that some things are to happen whose happening and whose course is unbound from all necessity.

For I think no one will say this: I do not think anyone will want to say that: That the things which now happen were not going to happen before they happened. That those things were not future before they came to be, which now come to be.
These things, then, even though foreknown, have free outcomes.

Even when foreknown, those things kept their free occurrence. For just as knowledge of present things imposes no necessity on the things that are happening, so foreknowledge of future things imposes no necessity on the things that are going to happen. Just as knowledge does not compel present things, so their foreknowledge does not compel future things either.
THAT GOD HAS NO MERE OPINION ABOUT FUTURE THINGS, ALTHOUGH THEY DO NOT HAPPEN UNDER COMPULSION; AND WHAT DECEIVES US IN THESE MATTERS. But, you say:
So you say: this very point is in doubt, whether there can be any foreknowledge of things that do not have necessary outcomes.

About this very point there is doubt: whether there can be any foreknowledge of things that do not happen by necessity. For they seem to be in conflict. They seem to you to be in conflict. And you think that if they are foreseen, necessity follows. And you think that if they are foreknown, they must happen by necessity. If necessity is lacking, they are not foreknown at all. If there is no necessity in them, there is no foreknowledge of them. And you think that nothing can be grasped by knowledge except what is certain. And you think there is knowledge of nothing except what is certain.
But if things whose outcomes are uncertain are foreseen as though they were certain. And if things are foreseen as though certain when it is still uncertain how they will turn out,
that is the darkness of opinion, not the truth of knowledge. You want to call that opinion, not knowledge. For you believe it is something different from the soundness of knowledge

to think otherwise than the thing actually is. To think otherwise than it is: you do not dare to count that as complete knowledge. The cause of this error is this: This error comes from the following: that everyone supposes that all things are known only from the power and nature of the things that are known. People think that each and every thing is known from its own nature. But the whole is the opposite. That is entirely the other way round. For everything that is known, all that is known, not according to its own power,

but is rather grasped according to the capacity of those who know it. It is not known according to its own power; rather, it is grasped according to the ability of the knowers. God does not see future things according to their power, but according to his own ability. That they are future is true of them in themselves, because they have not yet come. To him they are present, without any coming. Whatever anyone does in our presence is not necessary from the doer's side, yet it is necessary in that we see it. What God looks upon is likewise necessary in that he looks upon it. But the one who is still to do it in the future does it then without necessity. She [Philosophy] now begins to teach us this slowly, by examples.
SHE TRIES TO LEAD US FROM HUMAN KNOWING TO DIVINE KNOWING, BEGINNING WITH THE OUTER SENSE. For, to make this clear by a brief example:

Now listen here, so that an example of it may readily be given to you. "Sight recognizes the same roundness of a body in one way, and touch in another." If you are to perceive a round body, the eye perceives its roundness differently from the finger. "The one, remaining at a distance and casting its rays, beholds the whole at once." The eye shoots its glance there from afar and perceives the shape all together. "But the other, clinging to the sphere and joined to it, and moved around its circumference, grasps the roundness part by part." But the finger, laid upon it and moving all around it, explores it all piece by piece.
THAT THE OUTER SENSE AND THE OTHER, INNER WAYS OF CONSIDERING THINGS DIFFER FROM ONE ANOTHER. "Man himself, too, is beheld in one way by sense, in another by imagination, in another by reason,

in another by intelligence." These four senses just named do not perceive the same man in the same way. "For sense judges the figure as it is set in the underlying matter." The outer sense, such as sight, perceives the shape on something. "Imagination, however, judges the figure alone, without matter." The inner sense, which is called imagination, perceives the shape by itself, without the matter in which it previously saw it. "Reason, however, goes beyond this." But the sense that is called reason surpasses imagination. "And it weighs, by a universal consideration, the very form that is present in individual things." And it recognizes collectively the shape that appears singly on something. In the noun homo ("man")

is understood all together what is seen singly and individually in Plato, Cicero, and Socrates, and what also comes to mind individually without them. "But the eye of intelligence stands higher." The eye of intelligence looks out over these three senses. "For, having passed beyond the compass of the universal," because it surpasses the circuit of the collective, which reason grasps, "it beholds that simple form itself with the pure sight of the mind." It sees with a clear eye the simple image of God, which is simple because it is [not?] in underlying matter, as nothing else is [?]. It also sees in man the deeds that are certain to God, though they may be uncertain to the man himself, and that happen by necessity on the side of God's foreknowledge, but without necessity on the man's side.

With the outer senses we perceive outer things, that is, bodies, which he calls matter. And on the bodies, or together with the bodies, we perceive corporeal things, that is, their accidents: on them are colors and figures, and together with them, their actions. Imagination follows the senses. That is the mind's forming of images, without the bodies, just as the eyes saw them on the bodies or the ears heard them. So it may be that it previously saw a three-cornered shape, or a four-cornered one, or a round one, or the image of a man, or of a bird. Or it saw a race, or wrestling, or white, or black.

If the same likeness comes to a person in dreams, that is called phantasma and illusio (illusion). If he forms an image of it in his mind, that is called imaginatio (imagination). The beasts have these two in common with us, that is, sense and imagination. Ratio (reason) is the power of the mind that man alone has. It lets him know what he never saw, and what no image can be formed of. It teaches him to tell true from false and good from evil, and to infer one thing from another: he infers secondary substances from primary substances, the part from the whole and the whole from the part, the present from the past, and the future from the present. The pagan philosophers could understand nothing beyond the point to which reason led them. For this reason they held

that only those things were to be believed which were supported by reason, in this form: "If this is, then that is," or "If these things are, then that will be." This is why Aristotle said in the Categories that a privation cannot be changed back into a possession (habitus), so that a toothless person would get teeth again, or a forehead would grow hair again after baldness, because he knew of no reason by which this could happen. So it happened to some people, when heavenly wisdom came and invited them to divine understanding and told them to believe in the resurrection of the dead and that all things are possible for God, that they stumbled at this. They were darkened by the very thing that should have enlightened them. If you want to say, "Wherever there is reason,

there is also understanding (intellectus)," that is entirely true. Where there is human reason, there is also human understanding. But divine understanding and divine contemplation is simple and spiritual, because God himself is a simple spirit. Whoever recognizes this has a share in that same understanding. It teaches him that God is substance beyond substance, and form without form, without place and without time. He made the world without matter, he has a Son without otherness, and the Spirit proceeds from him without motion. Those who tried to apply human reason to these things became heretics.
THE LOWER IS COMPREHENDED BY THE HIGHER, NOT THE HIGHER BY THE LOWER. In this, that point must be considered most of all. In this

is what must be considered most carefully of all. For the higher power of comprehension takes in the lower. I mean that the higher faculty of perception grasps the lower one. But the lower in no way rises to the higher. The lower does not reach up to the higher. For sense has no power outside matter. That is, sense has no activity without a body, as imagination has. Of necessity we must see and touch the accidents of bodies on the bodies themselves. Nor does imagination behold universal forms. That is, the mind's power of forming images can picture the single image that it saw, but it cannot picture the common image, because it never saw it. How then could it perceive it either? Nor does reason grasp the simple form. Reason does not reach the simple image of God. It can only lead us to the forms that lie in substances.

and they are not substances but accidents. But the image of God is an image through itself, a supersubstantial substance, that is, prior to the substances which stand under accidents. But intelligence, as if looking down from above at the form it has conceived, also judges all the things that are beneath it. The intellect, as standing higher and looking upon the form known to it, discerns the lower things thoroughly. But it does so in the same way in which it comprehends the form itself, which could be known to nothing else. It sees the lower things in the same way in which it sees the form, which none of the lower ones sees. What is that way?
For it knows both the universal of reason and the figure of the imagination,
and the material sensible thing, using neither reason, nor imagination, nor the senses. It knows what reason and imagination and sense know, yet without relying on any of them.

Rather, it looks out over all things with that single stroke of the mind, formally, so to speak. With one glance it knows them all, in its own way, in the way in which it knows the form. Just as Benedict saw this whole world all together with a godly eye. Reason, too, comprehends imaginable or sensible things, using neither imagination nor the senses, when it looks at something universal. Reason also knows what the lower powers know, yet without relying on their powers, in order to see the universal. For it is reason that defines the universal it has conceived, thus. It is reason that shows the universality it has grasped, in these words:
"Man is a two-footed, rational animal." Man is a living thing, two-legged, rational. Although this notion is universal,

yet no one is unaware that it is a thing that can be imagined and perceived by the senses. Although the knowledge is universal, who does not know that it can also be pictured and seen? Reason does not consider this in imagination or sense, but in rational conception. It knows this nevertheless not by picturing or seeing, but by thinking rationally. Imagination also, although it took from the senses its starting point for seeing and forming figures, (although the power of forming images arises from the five senses), nevertheless, when sense is absent, surveys all sensible things. It still explores all visible images without sense.

It judges not by a sensible reasoning but by an imaginative one. It does not do so with the skill of the sense, but with its own skill. Do you see, then, O Boethius, how all things in knowing use their own faculty rather than that of the things that are known?

Do you not see now how all faculties of perception know more from their own power than from the power of the things known? And not wrongly. And rightly so. For since every judgment is the act of the one judging, it is necessary that each should accomplish his own work not by another's force but by his own power. For it is a great necessity, since choosing is the deed of the one choosing, that each should always perform his deed with his own strength, not with another's strength.
WHETHER THE STOICS ARE TO BE BELIEVED, WHO SAY THAT EMPTY MINDS ARE AFFECTED BY EXTERNAL BODIES. Once the Porch, that is, at Athens, brought forth, that is, had,
exceedingly obscure old men. The Porch: the great hall at Athens.

[?] formerly, the very deep-thinking old men, that is, the Stoic philosophers. Plato, the Athenian philosopher, lived at Athens in the villa Academia, which was his own property, and taught his disciples there until his death. After his death they split up. Some stayed there and were called Academics. Some began to walk about and were called Peripatetics. Some went into the city of Athens and were called Stoics. They got that name from the stoa, that is, the portico, where they sat and thought about their wisdom. "Who believe," that is, who believed, that sensations and images are impressed on minds
from external bodies. They held that these are impressed on every person's mind:
sensations and images, from the external bodies. People and trees,
