mountains and rivers, and all the bodies that are outside us, make us perceive in five ways. What would we perceive if they did not exist? What could we see or touch without bodies? And if their images did not exist, what would we then picture in our minds?
Coming from the bodies, they press into the mind. Their way in is

through the senses. How are they impressed on our minds? They do it in this way: we are acted on by them, not they by us; they act on us, not we on them. They give us sight and hearing, even though people say that we see and hear them.

"As it was once the custom to fix pressed letters with a quick stylus on the surface of a page that has no marks on it." That is, as letters are scratched with a stylus on a blank tablet. The tablet is like the mind, the stylus like the bodies, and the letters like the image.
[Heading:] THAT THE MIND EXERCISES ITS OWN POWER, YET IS OFTEN STIRRED FROM OUTSIDE, AND THEN MIXES THE INNER FORMS [WITH THE OUTER ONES]. "But if the mind unfolds nothing
by the vigor of its own motions" [Heading continued:] WITH THE OUTER ONES. But if the mind has no power and does nothing by its own activity,
"but only lies there passive," and it merely lies idle,
"subject to the marks of bodies," that is, subject to the images of the bodies that come upon it,
"and like a mirror gives back empty images of things," that is, like a mirror it reflects back the images of the bodies, copying them, if it can do nothing more:
"Where does this awareness that discerns all things get its power in minds?" That is, where then does the mind's knowledge, which perceives all things, come from?
"What power looks at individual things?" That is, which of its powers observes each thing separately so exactly?
"Or what power divides the things it knows,

and what power gathers again the things it has divided?" That is, which power divides the genera it knows into species, and then gathers them back into the groups of their genera? If the mind knows nothing more than visible things, how then does it know genera and species, which are not visible?
"And taking each path in turn,
it now raises its head to the highest things,

now comes down to the lowest." That is, taking a journey that alternates back and forth, is it at one time among heavenly things and at another among earthly things? It deals in turn with physical and theological questions. Reason makes people natural philosophers; understanding makes them theologians.
"Then, turning back to itself,
it refutes false things with true ones." That is, it then examines itself and puts out false arguments with true ones.
"This cause is more effective
and far more powerful." That is, this power is more effective and much mightier
"than that cause
which receives the marks pressed upon it!

in the manner of matter. Then the power of the mind, which bears the images imprinted on it, just like wax, or water, or mirror-glass, in which the images appear. Yet an affection takes place first in the living body,
stirring and moving the powers of the mind.
Now something from outside still meets the senses first, stirring and rousing the powers of the mind. When is that?
When light strikes the eyes,
or a voice sounds in the ears. That is, when someone sees or hears something.
Then the vigour of the mind, roused. Then at once the power of the mind, roused, calling
the forms that it holds within to similar motions,
applies them to the outward marks. It brings the inner images out toward certain motions [?], offers them, and moves them toward those same signs. And it mixes the images
with the forms stored away within.

And it mixes those that come from outside with the images kept inside it. The soul has all natural melodies and all modes within itself. When it hears them sung, they please it, because they are like it. It gladly admits to itself the proportions out of which it is joined together, as is written in the books on music. And by offering them toward the outward ones, it mixes two like things into one. Thus, because the tyrant of Babylon also had some image of the deity in his mind, he said when he looked at the outward image: "I see a man like the son of God." And the magicians in Egypt, because they had some knowledge of God, recognized the finger of God in the miracles of Moses.

AS WITH OUR MIND, SO ALSO THE JUDGMENT OF THE DIVINE MIND DOES NOT COME FROM A POWER OUTSIDE ITSELF. But if the mind is not marked, that is, instructed, by an affection when it perceives bodies; if, I say, it is not marked by an affection when it perceives bodies, — If the human mind, in understanding bodies, is not taught by their impact when it perceives the bodies themselves through their images, — but judges by its own power the affection that is subject to the body, that is, the image presented to the senses of its body. — but instead judges by its own power the things that meet its eyes and its ears. Now an inserted line of reasoning follows. Although qualities presented from outside affect the instruments of the senses, — Even though the images that meet them from outside come upon the eyes and the ears, with which we see and hear,

and an affection of the body, that is, of the bodily senses, comes before the vigour of the active mind, — and the impact on its senses comes before the power of its mind, which works through itself, — which calls forth the act of the mind in itself, — this impact rouses the act of the mind in itself, — and stirs up the forms that rest within in the meantime. — and stirs up the images inside it that until then still lay hidden. The inserted reasoning goes up to this point.
How much more do those beings that are free from all affections of bodies

not follow objects presented from outside when they discern, but carry out the act of their own mind. How much more is this true of the heavenly substances, which are free from all impact of bodies? In them it is evident that they do not follow outward things when they discern, but show the power of their own understanding.
THE DISTRIBUTION OF THE KINDS OF KNOWING. In this way, then, the many kinds of knowing have been allotted to diverse and different substances. In this way the various senses

have been allotted to various substances. In this way they have divided themselves among them. For sense alone, without the other kinds of knowing, has been allotted to living creatures that cannot move.

Sense alone has been allotted, without the other three senses, to those animals that cling fast somewhere. Such are the shellfish of the sea, and other creatures that are nourished while clinging to rocks. Sea mussels do this, and other creatures of the same kind, clinging to the stones. These only have the faculty of feeling. But imagination has been allotted to animals that move. Imagination has been added to the other living and moving creatures. These already seem to have the impulse to flee or to seek. I mean those that feel desire and aversion. This is why the ape imitates what it sees people do. If it had not first formed an image of it in its mind, it could not imitate it. But reason belongs only to the human race.

just as intelligence belongs only to the divine. Reason has been given only to human beings, just as intellect belongs to God alone. So that kind of knowing surpasses the others. So understanding must be the foremost. It knows by its own nature not only its own object, but also the objects of the other kinds of knowing. By itself it knows not only itself, but also the three lower ones.

THAT TWO KINDS OF KNOWING CANNOT CONTEND WITH THE THIRD. What, then, if sense and imagination oppose reasoning? What if the two lower faculties begin to contend with reason, saying that the universal is nothing

which reason thinks it perceives? They would say that the universal that reason thinks it knows does not exist. For what can be sensed or imagined cannot be universal. They would also say that things one can see or imagine as individuals cannot come together into one commonality. For Socrates and Plato and Demosthenes never together acquire one common image that one could see. Therefore either the judgment of reason is true and nothing can be sensed. They would also say that one of two things must be the case: either what reason thinks is true, and they themselves have been deceived about what can be seen; or, because they know that many things are subject
to the senses and the imagination, or because the things one can see and imagine are well known to them, the concept formed by reason is empty.
Then reason's opinion would be deceived. Reason considers what can be sensed and is individual as if it were something universal. Reason believes that

what can be seen and is individual is universal. Suppose reason answers this in reply. It would say that it does indeed perceive, in its grasp of the universal, what can be sensed and what can be imagined. It would say that, in reasoning about the universal, it knows well what both of them know. But they cannot rise to knowledge of the universal. Neither of them knows the universal itself.
For their knowledge cannot go beyond bodily shapes.

Because they cannot step beyond the outward images. But it must rather be believed that, concerning the knowledge of things, the firmer and more perfect judgment [is to be followed]. Therefore, where one argues about their three kinds of knowing, one should rather believe the more certain and more complete judgment. In a dispute of this kind, then, would we not rather approve the cause of reason, we in whom there is the power of reasoning as well as of imagining, and also of sensing? Would we not stand by reason in this dispute, we who are able to do both: to reason, and also to see and to form images? As it itself knows.

THE THIRD MUST ALSO BE JUDGED UNEQUAL TO THE FOURTH. It is similar, too, that human reason thinks the divine intelligence does not behold future things except [as it itself knows them]. So it stands, that human reason supposes that God's mind knows future things in no other way than reason itself knows them. For thus you argue.
For thus you argue: If any things appear not to have certain and necessary outcomes, they cannot be foreknown as certainly going to happen.

Whatever things are uncertain and are to come about without necessity, those cannot be foreknown as certainly going to happen. Therefore there is no foreknowledge of these things. And you say that there is no foreknowledge of things of this kind. But if we nevertheless believe that it exists, there will be nothing that does not come about from necessity. And if we are to believe in it, then nothing happens without necessity.
Therefore, if we could have the judgment of the divine mind, just as we are partakers of reason. If we could have the discernment of the divine mind, just as we are rational beings.
We would think it most just that human reason should submit itself to the divine mind, just as we judged that imagination and sense ought to yield to reason.

Then it would seem equally right to us that our reason should yield to God's mind, as we judged that sense and imagination must yield to reason. Therefore, if we can, let us be raised up to the summit of that highest intelligence. Therefore let us try to lift ourselves up, if we can, to that height of the foremost intelligence. For there reason will see what it cannot behold in itself. Then reason will find there

what it does not have in itself. And this is it. I mean this: in what way foreknowledge sees as certain and definite even those things that have no certain outcomes; how God's foreknowledge holds as certain and precisely determined those things that in themselves have no certain outcome. And [it will see] that this is not opinion; and that it is no supposition. But rather the simplicity of the highest knowledge, enclosed by no limits; rather, simple knowledge, having no measure and bounded by no borders.
THAT A MAN WHO HAS AN UPRIGHT BODY OUGHT ALSO TO BE RAISED UP IN MIND. In what varied shapes living creatures move across the lands! Of how many shapes
are the animals that travel about the world. For some have bodies stretched out and sweep the dust. Some move by stretching themselves out
and wiping the earth. And they draw a continuous furrow, driven on by the force of their breast. And they make an unbroken track, going on their breasts.
There are some whose roaming lightness of wings
both beats the winds and swims through the spaces of the vast ether in liquid flight. There are others that beat the wind with their wings and glide far and wide in the clear air.
These rejoice to have pressed their footprints on the ground. Some tread the earth with their feet. And they rejoice either to cross the green fields with their steps
or to go into the woods. So they wander about on foot, in wood and in field.
Though you may see all these differ in their various forms.

Though you see all these differ from one another in their shape. Yet their downward-bent face can weigh down their dull senses. But their head, hanging down, makes them have dull wits. In this they are not different from one another.
Only the human race lifts its lofty head higher.
Man alone lifts his head up. And he stands lightly with upright body and looks down on the earth. And he raises himself lightly all the way up, looking away from the earth.
This figure admonishes you, earthly one, unless you are foolishly witless. This image admonishes you, man, if you can understand it.
You who seek heaven with upright face and lift up your forehead,
lift your mind on high as well. You who look straight at heaven

and lift your head up, lift up your mind also. Lest, while the body is raised higher, the weighed-down mind sink lower to its ruin. Lest, with the body upright, the burdened mind sink down to perdition.
WHAT THE DIVINE STATE IS. Since, therefore, everything that is known is known not from its own nature but from the nature of those who comprehend it,

as was shown a little before. Since all known things are known not from their own nature but from the nature of those who know them, as we also said before. Let us now consider, as far as is permitted, what the state of the divine substance is. So let us now look, as far as we are able, at what state God's substance has. So that we may also be able to know what its knowledge is. So that we may also perceive what kind of knowledge his is. It is, then, the common judgment of all who live by reason that God is eternal. That God is eternal is the common belief of all rational beings. All of them have accepted that.
Let us therefore consider what eternity is. Now let us see what eternity is. For it reveals to us at the same time the divine nature
and the divine knowledge. By it, it teaches us to know God's nature and God's knowledge. Eternity, then, is

the whole, simultaneous and perfect possession of unending life. Eternity is the full and simultaneous possession of endless life. This becomes clearer from a comparison with temporal things. That is shown more plainly by comparison with things that exist in time.
THAT WHAT RUNS ON IN TIME, EVEN IF THAT TIME IS INFINITE, IS NOT ETERNAL. For whatever lives in time moves forward from the present into the future.

For whatever lives in time runs from the present into the future. And there is nothing placed in time that can embrace the whole span of its life all at once. Nor is there any non-eternal thing that can grasp its entire life all at once. But it has not yet grasped tomorrow, and it has already lost yesterday. But tomorrow is still ahead of it, and yesterday has already slipped away from it. And in today's life as well. And in today's life, which lies between yesterday's and tomorrow's,
you live no more. You do not live any more than in that moving and passing moment.

Than in the unstable and fleeting point. We do not live in the past (preterito), nor in the future (futuro); in the present (presenti) we always are. Nor can we stand still in that very present. As it comes, it runs away. And if anyone wants to point it out to another, he can say only once, and barely, "It is now." The very next time he must say, "It was now," if he is to point out that same moment. Such is our present. Whatever, therefore, undergoes the condition of time: that which must always suffer the created span of time. Even though it never began to be and never ceases, as Aristotle judged of the world: though it has no beginning and no ending, as Aristotle believed of this world. And though its life is stretched out with the infinity of time: and though its life stretches out with the endlessness of time, that is, of past, present and future.
Yet it is not such that it may rightly be believed to be eternal.

That is still not such that it may rightly be called eternal. For it does not comprehend and embrace all at once the whole extent of its life, even though that life is infinite: because it does not grasp all at once, as the eternal does, the whole breadth of its life, though its life has no end. But it does not yet have the future, and it no longer has the past: rather, one time lies before it and the other is gone.
That, therefore, which comprehends and possesses all at once the whole fullness of endless life,

but that which possesses all at once and holds within itself the whole extent of its endless life, so that nothing of the future is absent from it and nothing of the past has flowed away: so that nothing of what is to come is absent from it, and nothing that has passed has slipped away from it. That is rightly said to be eternal: that is rightly called eternal. And it must be in possession of itself: and of that one must say that it has power over itself. And be present to itself: and be its own presence to itself. And hold as present the infinity of moving time: and hold as present all the endlessness of running time. Therefore some people think wrongly: for this reason those people think wrongly
who think, when they hear that it seemed to Plato that this world neither had a beginning in time nor will have an end: those who think this,

when they hear it said that this world did not seem to Plato to have a beginning in time, or an end, that the created world is in this way made coeternal with its Creator: that this created world is in that way equally eternal with the Creator. For it is one thing to be carried through an endless life, which Plato attributed to the world: for to have life without end, which Plato granted to the world, is one thing. It is another to have embraced all at once the whole presence of endless life: it is another to have grasped all at once the whole presence of the ever-enduring life. This is clearly proper to the divine mind: this is plainly proper to the mind of God.
Nor should God be thought older than created things by quantity of time,
nor should God seem to us to come before his creatures in age of time, but rather by the property of his simple nature: but rather in the simplicity of his nature that is proper to him.

THE LONG DURATION OF TIME IMITATES ETERNITY. For that endless motion of temporal things imitates this present state of unmoving life. This endless course of the world strives to imitate that very state of present life, of life that always stands fixed. And since it cannot reproduce it and equal it, and since it cannot imitate it or make itself equal to it, it falls away from immobility into motion. So instead it gives up steadfastness and passes into unsteadiness.
And from the simplicity of the present it shrinks into the infinite quantity of the future

and the past. And from that simple presentness it falls into the endless multiplicity of past time and of future time. And since that motion of time cannot possess the whole fullness of its life all at once, and since that same course cannot grasp all the fullness of its life together, as eternity does, it seems in some measure to emulate what it cannot fulfil and express, by the very fact that it never ceases to be in some manner. So, by always enduring, it seems in some part to imitate that to which it still cannot fully make itself equal. It binds itself to whatever kind of presence this small and fleeting moment has, holding itself to the presentness, of whatever worth it may be [?], of this small

and fleeting moment. And since that presence bears a certain image of that abiding presence, since it somewhat images that presentness which stands fixed, that same presence grants to whatever things it touches that they seem to be. It gives to those things it is present to that they seem to exist. But since it could not remain, because it could not after all be steadfast,
it took up the infinite journey of time.

It took up the course in which no end comes in time. When the course ceases, time too has ceased. And so it came about that it continued its life by going on. And so it happened that it made its life continuous by moving, since it could not embrace the fullness of that life by remaining. It could not grasp that life all together by standing fixed. Therefore, if we wish to give things fitting names, following Plato, if we now rightly wish to give things fitting names after Plato, let us say that God is eternal and the world perpetual. Let us say that God is eternal and the world everlasting.
HAVING SET THESE THINGS OUT, TO SOLVE THE QUESTION Since, therefore, every judgment comprehends the things subject to it

HE TURNS. according to its own nature. Because every act of judging judges what is before its eyes according to its own power. And God has always an eternal and present state. And because God has an eternal and present state, his knowledge also, surpassing every motion, that is, the course of time, remains in the simplicity of its presence. So his knowledge too must necessarily abide in that simple presentness, rising above every change of time. If that same presentness did not grasp all things together, it would not be simple. Therefore he says immediately afterwards: And embracing the infinite spans of past and future. And embracing together the endless expanses of past and future.

It considers all things in its simple knowledge, as if they were happening now. It sees all things in its simple knowing, both those that are past and those still to come, as if they were always being done in the present.

THAT IT IS MORE PROPER TO GOD TO KNOW AND TO PROVIDE THAN TO FOREKNOW AND TO FORESEE. Therefore, if you wish to weigh the presence by which he discerns all things: if you wish to consider his presence, from which he knows it all, you will not judge it to be foreknowledge, as of something future. Then you will not say that he has foreknowledge, as of something to come, but more rightly knowledge of a never-failing present. Rather, it is more rightly knowledge of his unfailing presence. Hence it is called not foresight (praevidentia) but rather providence (providentia). Therefore it is not called fore-sight, but rather a far-reaching over-sight.

Because, set apart from the lowest things, it looks out upon all things as if from the lofty summit of things. Because it stands far from the lower things, it looks down on them all from far above, as if from the highest peak of the world.
THAT THE THINGS THAT ARE SEEN DO NOT BECOME NECESSARY FROM GOD'S SEEING [the heading continues in the next passage]. Why then do you demand that the things become necessary

JUST AS THEY DO NOT FROM OUR SEEING [end of heading]. which are illuminated by the divine light? Why do you think that necessity is imposed on the things that God's eyes look upon, when not even human beings make necessary the things they see?
For does your gaze add any necessity to the things that you perceive as present?

Does it, then? Does your looking impose any necessity on the things you see? By no means. It does not. And yet, if there is a fitting comparison between the divine present and the human: truly, if any fitting comparison can be made between man's presence and God's. Just as you see certain things in this temporal present of yours, just as you see certain things directly in this transitory present of the world, so he perceives all things in his eternal present. So he sees them all in his eternal presence. Therefore this divine foreknowledge does not change the nature and the property of things. Therefore this foreknowledge of God does not change the nature and the particular property of things.
And he beholds things as present before him in the same way as they will come forth at some time
in time as future things. And he sees them now as present to himself in the same way as they will still come at some time in the future.

THAT GOD PERCEIVES AND DISTINGUISHES WHAT IS NECESSARY AND WHAT IS NOT NECESSARY. Nor does he confuse the judgments of things, that is, of merits. This answers what you said earlier: that once free will is lost, neither vices nor virtues are anything, and there is only a mixed and undistinguished confusion of all merits. And he does not confuse his judgments, as you accuse him of doing, but he distinguishes the merits. And with one glance of his mind he discerns both what will come about necessarily and what will not come about necessarily. And in one glance of his mind

he sees the things that are to come by necessity and those that come without necessity. Just as you, when you see at the same time a man walking on the earth and the sun rising in the sky. So you also do: when you see together the man walking on the earth and the sun rising up in the sky. Although both are seen at once, you nevertheless distinguish them. Though you see both together, you still tell them apart. And you judge the one to be voluntary and the other to be necessary. And you consider the one to happen by necessity, the other without necessity. Thus, therefore, the divine gaze, looking down on all things, does not at all disturb the quality of things. So does God's eye: looking upon everything from above, it does not confuse the nature of things.
present with respect to himself, but future with respect to the condition of time.

Present to him, but future as far as time is concerned. From this it follows that this is not opinion, but rather knowledge resting on truth. Therefore this is no supposition for him, but true knowledge. When he knows that something will come to be, which he likewise is not unaware lacks the necessity of existing. When he knows that it will be in the future, which can nevertheless be without necessity, that is, when it comes in the future.
[Heading:] IF THE SYLLOGISM IS CONSTRUCTED IN THIS WAY, HOW IT IS TO BE ESCAPED. Here, if you say that what God sees will happen cannot fail to happen,

and that what cannot fail to happen happens of necessity. If here you want to say, as your proposition, that what God sees as future cannot be left undone, as is true; and, as your assumption, that what cannot be left undone must happen by necessity, which is also true. And to bind me to that name of necessity. And if you then want to force me, by your conclusion, to the name of necessity, thus: what God sees will happen, that happens of necessity. What God sees as future happens by necessity, since that too is true; what do I do then? I will indeed confess it to be a matter of most solid truth. Thus I acknowledge the truth so strengthened by the syllogism. But one which hardly anyone will reach, except a contemplator of the divine.

But of such a kind that hardly anyone would understand it, except one who is a beholder of divine things. For I will answer. I say plainly: The same future thing, when it is referred to divine knowledge, is necessary; but when it is weighed in its own nature, it appears entirely free and unconstrained. One future thing is both: necessary, when one looks to God's knowledge, and free and self-determining, when one looks to its own nature. Here the question is solved; this is the hidden knot that makes two contradictory things exist together in one thing.
[Heading:] EXPLANATION OF THE SAME STATEMENT, FROM THE FACT THAT THERE ARE TWO NECESSITIES, AS IS READ IN ARISTOTLE'S PERI HERMENEIAS. For there are two necessities.

There are two necessities. One is simple. One is simple and without condition. As, for example, that all men must be mortal. Like this one: that all people are necessarily mortal. The other is of condition. The other is with an 'if' and with conditions. As, if you know that someone is walking, it is necessary that he walks. Like this one: if you know that a man is walking, then it is necessary that he walks. For what anyone knows cannot be otherwise than it is known. What one knows, how can it be otherwise than as one knows it? But this condition by no means draws that simple necessity along with it.

But this conditioned necessity does not bring the bare necessity along with it. I mean, it does not follow that if he walks willingly, he therefore also walks against his will. For it is not its own nature that makes this necessity, but the addition of a condition. For nature does not produce this necessity; it comes from adding an 'if' to it. For no necessity compels a man who walks of his own will to go. For no necessity makes the man who walks willingly walk. Although it is necessary that he goes when he walks. However great the necessity that he goes while he is walking.
GOD'S PRESENT IS TO BE UNDERSTOOD FROM OUR PRESENT. In the same way, then, if providence sees something as present, that thing must necessarily be.

In the same way, whatever the present foresight looks upon must necessarily be so. Although it has no necessity of nature. Even though it has no natural necessity. But God beholds as present those future things that come about from freedom of choice. Indeed, God sees as present the things that are still to come from free will.

AGAIN IT IS REPEATED THAT THE NATURE OF FUTURE THINGS IS NECESSARY FROM ONE SIDE AND ABSOLUTE FROM THE OTHER. These things, then (that is, future things), when referred to the divine gaze, [The Latin text and the heading are interwoven in the source; the text sentence continues in the next passage.]
become necessary through the condition of divine knowledge.

That is the most necessary point about these things: that from the side of God's gaze they become necessary, according to the nature of God's knowledge, because his knowledge is like this. But considered in themselves, they do not lose the absolute freedom of their nature. But looked at by themselves, they do not lose the free liberty of their nature. So without doubt all the things that God knows will come do come about. Now all the future things that God foreknows truly come about without doubt. But some of them proceed from free will. Yet some of them still come from free will. And although these happen by coming into being. And however much they happen by coming into being,

they still do not lose their own nature. They still do not lose their nature. Because of that nature they could also have not happened, before they took place. Because of that nature they could also have come to nothing, before they happened.

AGAIN, ON THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN THE TWO NECESSITIES. What difference does it make, then, that they (that is, foreknown future things) are not necessary? What then sets them apart, so that they are not necessary? Since they come about in every way as if by necessity, because of the condition of divine knowledge. [The heading and the Latin text are interwoven in the source.]

Since they happen of necessity in every way, as it is laid down in God's knowledge? Because of that situation, they happen of necessity. This, namely, makes the difference. That distinguishes them. That which makes them differ, namely that those things that distinguish them, which I set forth a little earlier, which I gave as an example before. Which are they? The rising sun and the walking man. The rising sun and the walking man. Which, while they are happening,

cannot fail to happen. Those two cannot be left undone while they are happening. Yet of these, one had to exist of necessity before it happened, but the other not at all. The one had to come about of necessity before it came about; the other not of necessity.
So too, without doubt, those things will exist which God has present.

So too, without doubt, are the things that God has in His presence. But of these, one indeed comes down from the necessity of things, the other from the power of those who do them. But some of them come from necessity, some from the power of the doer. Therefore we said, not wrongly, therefore we said rightly, that these are necessary if they are referred to divine knowledge, that these are necessary when one looks to God's knowledge,
but that if they are considered in themselves, they are free from the bonds of necessity.

But when one considers them in themselves, they are unbound and not necessary. Just as everything that is plain to the senses is universal if you refer it to reason. Just so, any thing that one can see and touch is universal if one looks to reason. If you look at the things themselves, it is singular. And yet it is singular

if you pay attention to that. The things we look at are always single and individual, like Plato and Cicero and all individuals. Each of these same things is also universal, because it is a man, or an ox, or a horse, or wood, or stone. Because "this man" is also "man", he is therefore both singular and universal. The eye sees "this man"; reason knows only "man". Aristotle teaches this in the Categories.
IF A CHANGED WILL COULD ELUDE... But you will say: "Now it can happen," you say. "If... PROVIDENCE."

"...it lies in my power to change my purpose, I will make providence void, when perhaps I change the things it foreknows." "If it stands in my power to change my plan, then I overturn foresight, when I perhaps alter what it foreknows." I will answer.
To that I answer: You can indeed turn aside your purpose. You can certainly change your will.
But you cannot avoid the divine foreknowledge.

But you cannot escape God's knowledge or get away from it. For the present truth of providence sees that you can do this, because the present truth of foresight sees that you are able to do it, and whether you do it, and whether you do it, and where you turn, and also what you decide on. Just as you could not escape the gaze of a present eye, just as you also cannot escape the gaze of the eye of a man who is present, although you turn yourself by free will to various actions, though you turn yourself by your free choice to various deeds.
WHETHER FOREKNOWLEDGE COULD VARY AS THE WILL VARIES. "What then?" you will say. "How now?" you say. "Will divine knowledge be changed by my arrangement?"

Does God's knowledge then waver according to my disposition, which arises in me from time to time? "So that, when I want now this, now something else, it too would seem to alternate its turns of knowing?" That is, so that it would make changes in its knowing together with me, according as I want one thing at one time and something else at another? "By no means." It does not do that.
"For the divine gaze runs ahead of everything future." God's eye anticipates

all that is to come. "And it turns it back and calls it back to the presence of its own knowledge." And it turns it, and also turns it around, to the presence of its knowing. "Nor does it alternate, as you think, its turns of foreknowing, now this, now that." Nor does he change at all in his knowing, now this, now this, now that. "But remaining, it anticipates and embraces your changes at a single stroke." Rather, always standing steadfast, he catches your changes beforehand and embraces them with a single shot.
THAT GOD'S PROVIDENCE COMES FROM HIS SIMPLICITY, NOT FROM THE OUTCOME OF THINGS. "This presence of comprehending all things

and seeing them, God did not obtain from the outcome of future things." This ever-present presence of his beholding and encompassing all things he did not gain from what is going to happen. "But from his own simplicity." Rather, from his own simplicity, which understanding (intellectus) teaches us, not reason (ratio). "By this that point is also resolved which you put forward a little earlier." By this that too is answered

which you said before: "That it is unworthy if our future things are said to provide the cause of God's knowledge." That it would be unfitting if anyone were to think that our future things account for God's knowledge. "For this power of knowledge," this same power of his knowledge, "embracing all things with its present cognition,

embracing all things with its present knowing, "itself sets the mode for all things." It gives their manner to all things, not they to it. "And it owes nothing to later things." Nor does it have anything to thank those that come after for, as if it had learned it from them.

THAT FREE WILL STANDS, AND THAT REWARDS ARE DISPENSED ACCORDING TO MERITS. "Since these things are so, the freedom of the will remains unviolated for mortals." Because all this is so, their free will is not taken away from human beings.
"Nor do the laws unjustly set out rewards and punishments for wills that are released from all necessity." And the books of the law rightly promise free wills both reward and punishment.
"God also remains above as the onlooker of all things, foreknowing them."

And God is above, all-seeing and foreknowing. "And the eternity of his vision, always present, runs together with the future quality of our deeds." And the eternal presence of his sight corresponds to the future character of our works. "Dispensing rewards to the good, punishments to the wicked." Dispensing good to the good and evil to the evil. "Nor are hopes and prayers placed in God in vain." Nor are hope and entreaties placed in God to no purpose. "Which, when they are right, cannot be ineffective." They succeed when they are right.
EPILOGUE. "Therefore turn away from vices." Therefore loathe vices. "Cultivate virtues." Love virtues.
"Raise your mind to right hopes." Set your minds on right hope. "Offer humble prayers on high."

Send humble prayers up to heaven. A great necessity of uprightness is laid upon you, if you do not wish to pretend otherwise. Great need compels you to goodness, if you are willing to admit it. Since you act before the eyes of a judge who sees all things. For your deeds are watched over by the judge, who sees everything. Here we can see that after this fifth book Boethius was prevented by death, so that he could not hear from Philosophy what she had promised to tell him later. HERE ENDS THE FIFTH BOOK OF BOETHIUS THE CONSUL.
